candidats.titre: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
candidats.resume: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

candidats.titre: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics -- by Simon F. Lang, Matthew D. Gordon, Matthew J. Kotchen
candidats.resume: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

candidats.titre: Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence from the Democratization of Villages in India -- by Andrew D. Foster, Mark R. Rosenzweig
candidats.resume: We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly determine the effectiveness of development policies.

As a visitor who has stumbled upon the gathering by chance, I find the scene remarkably peaceful. The only reminders that the protests have not always been this way are three rubbish bins, apparently set alight out of habit and the façade of the Ministry of Education. It is against this façade that the anger of many Albanians has erupted – anger that has specifically Albanian roots on the one hand, but is also part of a broader European context, and for which Germany has long lacked any sustainable form of public expression. candidats.titre: Das pazifistische Grundgesetz und die „Zeitenwende“
candidats.resume: Wenn es um militärische Machtmittel aus verfassungsrechtlicher Perspektive geht, stehen Normen des Grundgesetzes im Mittelpunkt, die zwischen 1954 und 1968 in das Grundgesetz eingefügt worden sind. TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image. The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors. These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures. candidats.titre: Derrière les polémiques autour du terme « racisé », une opposition sur le poids du racisme dans notre société
candidats.resume: Quelle place joue la couleur de peau dans nos trajectoires de vie ? Khamkéo/Unsplash , CC BY L’ESSENTIEL Les polémiques sont nombreuses autour du terme « racisé », mais elles cachent un désaccord plus profond, portant sur la compréhension du racisme. L’enjeu, derrière le mot, porte donc sur la place que les phénomènes raciaux occupent, ou non, dans l’organisation de la société. Cette question est un enjeu académique et politique majeur qui mériterait plus de travaux de recherche et moins de positions caricaturales. La controverse sur le terme « racisé » resurgit régulièrement dans les médias, avec son lot de confusions et de malentendus. Mais s’agit-il véritablement d’une querelle terminologique ? Nous voudrions montrer que le terme « racisé » est aujourd’hui l’otage d’une controverse qui ne le concerne pas, qui porte sur la place à donner au racisme et aux autres phénomènes raciaux dans notre compréhension de la société et dans laquelle chaque camp tend à caricaturer la position adverse. « Racisé » enferme-t-il ceux qu’il désigne ? Commençons par nous intéresser à la critique du terme « racisé » qui s’est à nouveau fait entendre récemment dans la presse sous la plume du sociologue Stéphane Beaud et de l’historien Gérard Noiriel : ce terme « enfermerait » les personnes auxquelles il est appliqué. Cette critique nous semble manquer sa cible car, à lui seul, le terme « racisé » n’enferme pas plus qu’un autre terme pouvant servir à qualifier des personnes comme « cardiaque » ou « député ». En effet, ces termes ne font que nommer certaines caractéristiques que des personnes…

candidats.resume: De la fumée s’échappe du bâtiment du gouvernement ukrainien à Kiev, après une attaque russe dans la nuit du 7 septembre 2025. Service d’État pour les situations d’urgence d’Ukraine/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY , CC BY L’ESSENTIEL Aux États-Unis, les élections de mi-mandat ont infligé un revers cinglant à Donald Trump et aux républicains au Congrès. Peu de commentateurs croient que ce résultat changera beaucoup la politique de Trump envers l’Ukraine. Un accord entre « grandes puissances » sans Kiev se heurterait presque à coup sûr aux démocrates du Congrès. Les élections de mi-mandat ont modifié le rapport de force au Congrès des États-Unis, infligeant un revers cinglant à Donald Trump et à son Parti républicain. Ce résultat aura des conséquences dans le pays et peut-être aussi à l’étranger, notamment pour la politique de Washington envers l’Ukraine, un sujet quasiment absent des campagnes. Mais si l’ Ukraine a peu pesé dans le scrutin, la question de l’attitude à adopter face à la guerre n’a pas disparu de la vie politique états-unienne. De fait, dans les semaines et les mois qui ont précédé l’annonce des résultats, Trump s’était employé à revenir sur le soutien des États-Unis à l’Ukraine. Il l’a fait malgré une forte opposition, y compris dans les rangs républicains. La transmission à Kiev de renseignements cruciaux sur les frappes russes a été interrompue , avant d’être rétablie, tandis qu’une aide militaire essentielle était réduite. Trump a aussi décidé de suspendre plusieurs sanctions visant la Russie. Le président ukrainien Volodymyr Zelensky a dénoncé cette décision…

Democrats’ historic victories in this week’s U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry.
The public voted on 41 data center-related ballot measures on Tuesday — in all but one, the majority voted to impose more restrictions on data center development. And even when data centers weren’t on the ballot directly, they were a major talking point, with newly-elected Democratic governors and congressmembers likely to support additional regulation.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and Anthony Ha discuss what the election will mean for the tech industry moving forward — not just when it comes to data centers (which OpenAI is already trying to rebrand), but also increased government scrutiny of Big Tech.

Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO hits resistance as investors balk at valuation
Anthropic's IPO is in trouble as investors push back on the $1.5 trillion valuation and the tech market sells off. According to Reuters, potential backers doubt the planned roadshow can kick off next week as scheduled.
As recently as September, the company was eyeing a valuation of up to $2 trillion. Now some investors think even $1.5 trillion is too rich. One investor reportedly floated a valuation of just $1 trillion. Investors want a steeper discount because Anthropic is still losing money and burning through cash to scale its AI infrastructure. They're also waiting on October revenue numbers, which are missing from the updated S-1 filing.
The midterm elections made things worse. Ballot initiatives targeting data center expansion passed in several states, triggering the sharpest tech selloff in a year. The Wall Street Journal also reports that IPO investors are skeptical. If AI stocks stay under pressure, Anthropic could delay the offering, which some estimates peg at up to $100 billion in size. A delay could further shake confidence in the broader AI sector.

SOURCE 1 (The Decoder) :
Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small claims top spot among western open-weight models
Key Points
- Thinking Machines, the startup from former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, is releasing Inkling 2 Small, a mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion parameters, 17 billion of which are active at any given time.
- On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Inkling 2 Small scores 31, an 18-point jump over its predecessor and roughly on par with Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash, with especially strong gains in agentic tasks.
- The improved performance comes at a price, though. The model generates more output tokens and costs six times as much per task as its predecessor. It's initially available as a proprietary offering through the Tinker platform, with weights under an Apache license to follow.
Inkling 2 Small claims to be the strongest Western open-weight model, with 17 billion active parameters and benchmark scores that far exceed its predecessor.
The startup from former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, Thinking Machines, has unveiled Inkling 2 Small, its second model generation. Inkling models are designed as base models for fine-tuning, which could make them especially attractive for specialized applications.
The mixture-of-experts model contains a total of 594 billion parameters, of which 17 billion are active at any given time. It accepts text and images as input and offers an adjustable thinking depth that lets users choose between speed and thoroughness.
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Inkling 2 Small scores 31, according to Thinking Machines. That's 18 points above the predecessor Inkling Small (13) and roughly on par with Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash.
The biggest gains show up in agentic tasks, where the model independently executes multi-step workflows. On AutomationBench-AA the score jumps from 5 to 46 percent, and on FrontierCode 2.0 it rises from 5 to 25 percent. On the knowledge-work benchmark AA-Briefcase, Inkling 2 Small hits 1,527 Elo, 615 points above its predecessor. The hallucination rate drops from 61 to 27 percent, but largely because the model answers fewer questions. The response rate falls from 77 to 53 percent.
Costs rise but stay well below the competition
The better results come partly at the cost of higher token usage. Inkling 2 Small produces roughly 150,000 output tokens per task on average, about four times as many as its predecessor. At $1.18 per task it costs nearly six times as much, according to Artificial Analysis. That's still far cheaper than Gemini 3.8 Flash ($7.77) or Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($10.02), and it lands closer to the price range of low-cost Chinese models.
Thinking Machines says it trained the model with reinforcement learning on hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding tasks. An automated evaluation system checked whether the code worked and how the model approached each task. On FrontierCode 2.0, Inkling 2 Small reaches 25.4 percent, on DeepSWE 72.1 percent, and on SWEBench Pro v2 (Hard) 86.3 percent. The new Deepseek-V4.1-Flash still leads on most of those tests, hitting 28.5 percent on FrontierCode and 77 percent on DeepSWE.
Vision and design scores lead among open-weight models
Thinking Machines says the model is strongest in text recognition, infographic interpretation, and visual reasoning. On the document benchmark GDP.pdf, which tests whether models can answer questions from complex PDF documents, it scores 25.2 percent, the highest among the compared models. On MMMU Pro, a benchmark for multimodal understanding of academic tasks involving diagrams and figures, Inkling 2 Small reaches 81.6 percent.
On PerceptionBench, which tests the visual perception ability of multimodal models, it leads with 64.7 percent. For visual creation, the model earns a 1,340 Elo rating on DesignArena Website, where users rate AI-generated websites in head-to-head comparisons. That's the highest score among open-weight models. Thinking Machines says the model has also made progress in 3D modeling.
In a somewhat unusual demonstration, the team pitted the model against its own researchers in a blind wine tasting. Working from a photo alone, Inkling 2 Small correctly identified three wines in 19 out of 20 attempts.
Compact training run, open weights coming soon
The total training run is remarkably compact compared with the competition. Across all phases the model processed about 12 trillion tokens, according to Thinking Machines, far fewer than comparable rivals. The reinforcement-learning phase after base training needed only 3 trillion tokens on 2,048 GPUs over nine days.
Thinking Machines says the model sometimes communicates inefficiently, and that's likely a bigger issue, it doesn't always pick the best tools for large codebases. It doesn't support audio and is less optimized for chat. It can also overreact to health-related topics and produce cluttered output.
For now, Thinking Machines offers the model through its Tinker platform. The company plans to release the weights under an Apache 2.0 license once external safety testing wraps up. That's one of the most permissive open-source licenses and an advantage over more restrictive open-weight licenses such as those from Meta or Mistral. Thinking Machines says the model belongs to a family of different sizes, and the company plans to release more variants soon.

SOURCE 2 (ZDNET) :
ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Thinking Machines released a competitive new open model, Inkling 2 Small.
- Most competitive open models come out of China.
- The release follows French lab Mistral’s Le Chonk open model, which excels at coding.
Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.
Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot
Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
More from ZDNET
What Inkling 2 Small does
Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.
“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.
Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.
The open-weight race
Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.
French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.
Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding
“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.
But rarely is a model the full package.
“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.
Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.
Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.
“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

Frontier Radar #5: If AGI is so close, why is everyone leaving? The neolabs and their bets
OpenAI is talking about the AGI era, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AGI has arrived. At the same time, co-creators of today's models are leaving OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta to start their own labs, raising billions with no product to show. Why? They're betting that the current recipe alone won't be enough. We've sorted 45 neolabs by their research bets, mapped the limitations of today's AI they're trying to overcome, looked at what's already visible from their work, and explain why Nvidia always wins.
Six times a year, THE DECODER's editorial team takes a deep dive into a foundational AI topic in its "Frontier Radar" series, published as a newsletter and exclusively on the site for THE DECODER subscribers. Issue #5 profiles 27 AI labs in detail, sorted by six research bets, plus nearly 20 more in brief and an overview covering origins, valuations, and what's publicly available. Issue #1 covered the current state of agentic AI. Issue #2 examined the measurable impact of AI on productivity. Issue #3 covered the emerging token economy of generative AI. Issue #4 asked what's left of the AI lead over China and where Europe stands.
Dear readers,
After the launch of GPT-6 Astra, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared on X: "AGI has arrived." OpenAI president Greg Brockman called the model a turning point and welcomed humanity to the "AGI era". What exactly the two men mean isn't clear, since there's no agreed-upon definition of AGI. The message comes through anyway: an extremely powerful AI, possibly a self-improving one, is imminent and the path is mapped out.
Many of the people who built today's systems apparently see things differently. Dozens have left the big labs to start their own. Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI and served as its chief scientist; now he's building Safe Superintelligence. Jerry Tworek led the development of OpenAI's reasoning models and now runs Core Automation. David Silver, the mind behind AlphaGo, left Google DeepMind for Ineffable Intelligence. Yann LeCun left Meta after twelve years and founded AMI. Jeff Dean spent 27 years at Google, most recently as chief scientist, and started Discovery Loop.
The money follows: Nvidia invested in SSI in July, reportedly five billion dollars according to Bloomberg. The lab hasn't released a single model or paper. Prometheus, Jeff Bezos' industrial AI lab, pulled in twelve billion dollars at a 41 billion valuation in June. Flapping Airplanes has no public model either and raised one billion dollars in an October Series A.
The motives are mixed, and not all technical. At these valuations, founders become paper billionaires fast. LeCun left after a strategy dispute with Meta. Sutskever wants to do research without product pressure. Others want to carve out a niche that would be a sideshow at a big lab. Some departures aren't even a clean break: Google itself is a founding investor in Discovery Loop.
What many founders share is a doubt. Not about whether much more powerful AI is coming; some think AGI is close. Their doubt is about whether today's recipe alone gets there: ever-larger language models, trained on internet data, refined with reinforcement learning.
What is a neolab?
There's no official definition. We use the term for independently founded, research-driven AI companies that build their business around a long-term technical bet. They want to change how AI learns, perceives the world, solves problems, is controlled, or computes.
The current wave became visible in 2024. The race for the strongest models was in full swing, and the cloud giants had their partners: Microsoft backed OpenAI, Amazon backed Anthropic. Then Sutskever founded SSI in June and raised a billion dollars within months for a research team with no product.
There's a reason investors fund that. OpenAI and Anthropic have grown into corporations on the back of their success, and both are pursuing IPOs at record valuations. Internally, research teams compete with product teams for money and attention. Established companies struggle with ideas that threaten their business, management scholars call this the innovator's dilemma. That's what investors are betting on: a small team finds what the giants miss.
There are precedents. The Transformer was invented at Google in 2017. DeepMind beat the world's best Go players with AlphaGo. Yet the AI assistant for the masses came from OpenAI, founded as a nonprofit in 2015. The second breakout came from an OpenAI spinoff: Dario and Daniela Amodei founded Anthropic in 2021. By the end of July 2026, Bloomberg pegged its annualized revenue at over 65 billion dollars.
The real bet neolabs are making is on research gaps the big players don't fill, either because nobody knows the path or because nobody allocates resources for it. The big labs have more compute, established data pipelines, and feedback from hundreds of millions of users. What a small lab builds can show up at the market leader shortly after the first product ships.
TypeSafe AI shows how short a lead can be. In mid-September it launched Jev, a decision model. Two weeks later, OpenAI announced its Decisions API. But even a brief lead shows expertise and can pay off as an exit. Microsoft hired the core team from Inflection. Google grabbed the founders of Character.ai and the leadership of Windsurf. AMD wants to acquire World Labs for about 8.2 billion dollars. Nvidia is in talks with Reflection, according to the Financial Times.
For neolabs, it all comes down to one question: can they deliver something the big players don't have, something customers or the big players themselves will pay for? We selected 27 labs, most from the US and Europe, and sorted them into six groups by their primary bet.
Bet 1: A good problem solver isn't necessarily a good learner
Today's models can do remarkable things, but they learn differently from humans. They need massive amounts of data to pick up a skill, and once deployed, they typically don't update their weights. They can use new information within a conversation but don't permanently learn from every experience. Continual learning remains a central research gap. Six labs want to change that and attack the problem from three angles: learning during deployment (Adaption, Core Automation), learning from few examples (Flapping Airplanes, Ndea, SSI), and learning from experience (Ineffable).
Adaption bets against scaling
Sara Hooker led research at Cohere and previously worked at Google Brain. In 2020, she argued in "The Hardware Lottery" that research approaches often win not because they're better but because they fit the available hardware. In January she followed up with "On the Slow Death of Scaling", arguing that more compute leads to better models less and less reliably. Data and training methods are more effective levers. Open models with 8 or 27 billion parameters now beat the much larger Falcon 180B on benchmarks.
With Sudip Roy, she founded Adaption. According to them, they are betting against scaling and plan to build efficient AI that continuously learns instead. Rather than one big model for everyone, models should adapt to their users on the fly and cheaply. The first products tackle the most obvious lever, data: tools for cleaning, visualizing, and automated training via AutoScientist. The actual goal, a model that learns during deployment, is still missing.
Core Automation's insider search for new learning methods
Jerry Tworek spent almost seven years at OpenAI, most recently as vice president of research, leading the development of the reasoning models o1 and o3. His critique of today's recipe comes from someone who helped build it. Co-founder Rohan Anil led Gemini's pre-training at Google.
Retraining a trained network risks making it forget what it already knew. Researchers call this catastrophic forgetting. The Transformer wasn't built to learn on the fly during deployment either.
ChatGPT and Claude now take notes and retrieve earlier conversations as a workaround. Tworek doesn't think that's enough, as for him continual learning is a problem for machine learning, not for Markdown files, as he said. Core is looking for learning algorithms beyond pre-training and reinforcement learning, plus architectures that scale better. The first model is supposed to update its weights during deployment and get by with one hundredth of today's training data. So far, nothing more than rumors.
Core's first test is on itself: a small team with research agents aims to match the output of a large lab, for instance by having agents automatically generate efficient GPU code from an architecture idea.
This kind of research was barely possible at OpenAI, Tworek said after leaving. When you're in a race for the best model, you take fewer risks.
Flapping Airplanes wants to learn more from less data
Brothers Ben and Asher Spector founded Flapping Airplanes with Aidan Smith, previously at Neuralink. Ben is the lead author of ThunderKittens, a widely used GPU kernel library.
The thesis: today's models are strong where data is plentiful, like text and images. In fields like robotics or biology, where data is scarce and expensive, they fall short. Flapping Airplanes wants to build models that learn from few examples instead of needing massive datasets. The founders are looking for learning methods inspired by biological principles but designed to run on GPUs.
Nothing visible has come out yet. Most of the first year went into foundations: software that makes GPU training more efficient by cutting the usual overhead between many small compute steps. New learning methods have to run on existing hardware before they can work.
Investors don't mind the missing model. After 180 million dollars in January, an October Series A brought one billion at a six billion valuation.
Ineffable Intelligence wants to learn without human examples
David Silver isn't going after less data. He's going after different data. At Google DeepMind, he led the development of AlphaGo and its successors. The original AlphaGo still learned from human games. AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero learned only from self-play and surpassed all predecessors.
In spring 2025, Silver and Richard Sutton turned that insight into a program. In "Welcome to the Era of Experience", they argue that systems that only imitate humans can barely get past human-level performance on many important tasks. The next systems need to learn from their own experience, with rewards from the environment rather than from human judgment. Silver later founded Ineffable Intelligence. His goal is a "Superlearner" that learns from experience in both digital and physical environments.
The hardest question is where the feedback comes from. In Go, wins and losses decide. In science or the physical world, success is often unclear or shows up late. Reinforcement learning has always been strongest where the environment gives a clear signal. Ineffable has to prove it works for open-ended, changing tasks too. In April, the company announced a 1.1 billion dollar seed round at a 5.1 billion post-money valuation, the largest in Europe. There's no usable system.
Ndea wants to find rules from few examples
François Chollet developed Keras, a deep learning library, and designed the ARC benchmark, which measures how well systems figure out new tasks from just a few examples. After years at Google, Chollet is building Ndea with Zapier co-founder Mike Knoop. The team has about 15 people.
Chollet draws a line between ability and learning: a system can solve a task brilliantly because of extensive training and still be unable to pick up a new skill efficiently. Ndea uses program synthesis. The system searches for a program that explains the observed examples, with a neural model steering the search toward promising candidates. A few examples should yield rules that hold for new cases too.
Chollet's own benchmark is falling even without Ndea. On ARC-AGI-3, launched in March, GPT-6 Astra scored up to 99.9 percent in September, and 62.7 percent in the standard setup. The path there is telling: Astra translated unfamiliar game environments into compact rules and its own shorthand notation, roughly what Ndea is aiming for. Ndea hasn't posted its own ARC-AGI-3 result yet.
Safe Superintelligence has credibility but nothing to show
Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI and served as its chief scientist, co-authoring some of the most important papers in deep learning. He left in 2024 and founded SSI, where he's now CEO. The founding manifesto describes the goal: safe superintelligence, free from product distractions. About 50 employees in Palo Alto and Tel Aviv have published neither a model nor a paper.
Sutskever described his focus in late 2025 in a conversation with Dwarkesh Patel. Humans transfer what they've learned after a few examples, while models need massive datasets - and he plans to change that. He expects a system that learns as well as a human in five to twenty years.
In July, SSI and Nvidia announced a partnership to increase compute capacity tenfold. Bloomberg reported five billion dollars. SSI had research that deserved to be scaled up, Sutskever said in the joint announcement. Combined with the three billion raised earlier, that's roughly eight billion dollars. The last known valuation is 32 billion dollars. It rests mainly on Sutskever's reputation and the expectation that he sees a path others don't.
Other labs with a similar goal
Pathway in Palo Alto has already published an architecture for what Core Automation is targeting. Its BDH model adapts during processing, forming a kind of working memory. So far, this has only been shown with small models of up to one billion parameters.
Symbolica, founded in 2022, combines neural learning with program synthesis like Ndea but uses its own math-based architecture rather than language models. The founders themselves call the long-term goal, a general machine for program synthesis, unsolved. Symbolica earns money in the meantime with Agentica, a tool for building AI agents.
Bet 2: Language alone isn't enough
The first group wants to change how models learn. The second wants to change what they learn from. These founders doubt that language is the best path to intelligence. They want systems that understand spatial relationships, predict physical consequences, and act in the world. AMI predicts abstract states, Black Forest Labs predicts video frames and robot movements, General Intuition learns from video games, World Labs generates 3D worlds, and Physical Intelligence learns control directly on the robot.
AMI is Yann LeCun's counter-program
Yann LeCun received the Turing Award and built Meta's research lab FAIR. For years, he has argued against the idea that language models lead to human-like intelligence. He left Meta in late 2025 after strategic disagreements: the company wanted to focus on language models it could commercialize quickly. At AMI, LeCun is executive chairman. CEO is Alexandre LeBrun, founder of Nabla, a medical AI startup.
Technically, AMI builds on JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture), which LeCun proposed in 2022 as an alternative to generative language and video models. Instead of predicting outputs token by token, JEPA works with abstract internal representations. It learns what matters when predicting what comes next in a video or a robot's movement, without getting lost in pixel-level details. V-JEPA 2 showed the approach can work at Meta in 2025. After pre-training on video, just 62 hours of robot data was enough for robotic arms to handle simple pick-and-place tasks in unfamiliar labs, planning much faster than pixel-level approaches.
AMI is targeting industry, robotics, and healthcare, with Nabla as its first partner. In March, the lab raised 1.03 billion dollars at a 3.5 billion pre-money valuation with about a dozen employees. LeBrun says openly that a product could be years away. Research and most of the code are planned to be open.
Black Forest Labs goes from image generator to robot controller
Black Forest Labs from Freiburg is known for its FLUX image models, which already generate revenue. The founders, led by Robin Rombach, co-developed the method behind Stable Diffusion.
Since this fall, the lab is making a bet that goes beyond image generation. An image model has learned how images change, which means it can also learn what change a given action causes.
The first step is FLUX 3 Action, released in September. It builds on FLUX 3, a base model trained mainly on video, and was fine-tuned on data where the action behind each video is known: gameplay footage, first-person videos, teleoperated robots. The model takes a camera image, the robot's state, and a text instruction and predicts the next two seconds: how the robot should move and what the scene looks like afterward. It's an image generator that learned to control robots. The weights are on Hugging Face.
On RoboLab-120, a robotics benchmark from Nvidia, FLUX 3 Action ranked second behind Lakeside on October 22 and has since dropped to fourth. The testing is done in simulation, not on a real robot.
General Intuition turns gameplay into training data
General Intuition grew out of Medal, a platform for game clips. Medal CEO Pim de Witte founded it in 2025 with three researchers from the University of Geneva who had worked on world models for games.
The idea: record players' inputs alongside game video. The result shows not just what changed but what action caused the change. Medal provides billions of video frames paired with keyboard and mouse inputs. From these, the lab trains two types of models: world models that predict what happens next and action models that decide what to do.
The approach isn't entirely new. OpenAI trained a Minecraft agent on gameplay video with VPT in 2022. DeepMind connects Gemini with a 3D game agent through SIMA 2.
General Intuition plans to make money as a platform with API access to its models, for game studios and robotics companies alike. As proof, it showed a model trained solely on games controlling a quadruped robot after just eight minutes of fine-tuning with real robotics data.
Physical Intelligence builds a general model for robots
Physical Intelligence learns directly on the robot. The lab was founded by some of the biggest names in learned robotics, including Sergey Levine from Berkeley and Chelsea Finn from Stanford. Levine, previously at Google, describes the goal as a general robot model: a single system that works across many robots and many tasks. Nobody should have to program a separate controller for each task.
The π model family combines vision, language, and action. The lab collects most of its training data itself: humans teleoperate robots, and the model learns from the recordings. In April, π0.7 shipped with about five billion parameters. It combines learned skills into new tasks and matched individually trained specialist models in the lab's own tests. Since October 13, the Pi API is in beta: developers upload their own robot data, fine-tune the models, and run them from the cloud.
In March, reports surfaced about funding talks at more than eleven billion dollars in valuation. Competition comes from Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2, from other robotics startups, and potentially from generalists like Astra that already control robotic arms. More on that below.
World Labs builds spatial intelligence, soon under AMD's roof
Fei-Fei Li is a Stanford professor known for the ImageNet dataset. In 2024, she founded World Labs with three researchers from Meta and Google, including NeRF co-inventor Ben Mildenhall. Her topic is spatial intelligence: AI that understands and generates the three-dimensional world. 3D is the language of nature, according to Li.
Since November 2025, World Labs has been selling Marble. It creates editable 3D worlds from text, images, video, or sketches, and since January also via API. Game developers use it for prototyping, robotics researchers for training environments. Marble provides the stage; what happens when a robot bumps into a chair is still handled by the simulator. Atlas is meant to close that gap and has been available to select partners since September. Atlas generates, reconstructs, and simulates in one step: a few photos become a walkable space, plus up to one minute of video with controlled camera movement.
In late September, AMD announced plans to buy World Labs for about 8.2 billion dollars in stock. The deal is expected to close by end of 2026, with Li becoming AMD's chief scientist. AMD's official reason is gaining insight into applications, but there's likely more to it. Nvidia has a complete platform for physical AI with Omniverse, Isaac, and the Cosmos models. World Labs lets AMD close part of that gap.
Other labs with a similar goal
Odyssey in San Francisco shares the bet of World Labs and General Intuition: a world model that learns motion and physics from video should teach agents to act. Since September, up to 20 humans and AI agents can operate in the same simulated world in Agora-2, with no traditional game engine running underneath. Runway, known for video generators and older than the current wave, took the same path as Black Forest Labs in December 2025 with GWM-1: from video model to action-responsive simulation, all the way to robotics.
In robot control, Physical Intelligence has two close relatives. Skild AI in Pittsburgh also wants one model for many robots but learns first from simulations and internet video. At over 14 billion dollars in valuation, it's among the highest-valued companies in this space. Generalist collects its own robot data like Physical Intelligence and showed in August with GEN-1.5 how a robot learns short manual tasks from just a few demonstrations.
The generalists are catching up
General-purpose models are gaining ground fast, however. Their spatial understanding is growing: GPT-6 Astra models a house in Blender and makes it walkable in Unreal Engine. Gemini 4 Carbon reaches human-level performance on the 3D understanding benchmark Blueprint-Bench 2.
On real robots, some limits still show up. In the AA-Robotics benchmark, Astra controls a robotic arm through self-written code and leads with 69 out of 100 points but takes half an hour per task and costs over 16 dollars. A human takes 20 seconds. With even more compute, Astra surpassed the specialist models Lakeside and FLUX 3 Action in an Nvidia study, at about 36 dollars per task.
But there is a pattern: generalists can already beat specialists on certain tasks but need much more time and money to do it. Robotics researcher Georgia Chalvatzaki sees this as a real change in capabilities but not proof that scaling alone solves robotics. The most impressive results don't come from the model alone: Astra uses simulators, motion planners, existing control software, and reinforcement learning as tools.
Chalvatzaki's conclusion: generalists are getting better at using and combining existing robotics tools. But the tools themselves, fast controllers, physics models, safety layers, still need to be built. Whether that's good news for the specialists will become clear in the coming months.
Bet 3: The most valuable data isn't on the internet
The third group bets on data that doesn't exist online: measurements from laboratories, samples from nature, engineering data from factories. Better general models don't hurt them; they serve as building blocks. The edge is supposed to come from exclusive access. Three questions matter: who generates the data, who gets to use it, and how hard is it to replicate? Basecamp and Periodic already have parts of their datasets in place. Prometheus says it's building its own.
Basecamp Research mines genes from volcanoes and the deep sea
Basecamp Research in London was founded in 2019, making it older than the current wave. But it shows with particular clarity what's at stake, when there is no internet-scale data yet. This is the case for biology, according to Basecamp Co-founder Glen Gowers. Public gene databases mostly cover well-studied organisms. Basecamp collects its own samples with local partners in more than 30 countries: from rainforest soils, volcanic rock, and the deep sea. The dataset reportedly contains more than 100 billion previously unknown genes, and Basecamp controls access. The Trillion Gene Atlas, announced in March, is meant to massively expand the data, with Nvidia and Anthropic as partners.
On this data, Basecamp trains its EDEN model family. EDEN designs long DNA sequences along with the enzymes that insert them into the genome. Some features are available to researchers through Claude. The first application is cell therapies: six programs are in early research and development before clinical trials. Basecamp hasn't given a timeline for clinical trials.
Periodic Labs uses nature as a learning environment
Periodic Labs generates its own data. Liam Fedus led post-training at OpenAI. Ekin Dogus Cubuk ran the GNoME project at Google DeepMind, which predicted millions of new crystal structures in 2023. Only a few hundred have been confirmed in the lab so far. Their motto: Intelligence is necessary, but not sufficient. Scientific progress needs to be checked against reality.
That's why Periodic runs largely automated labs in Menlo Park. Robots mix powders, furnaces bake them, X-ray machines check the results around the clock. This produces data that's in no textbook, especially negative results. Journals publish the crystals that worked and they almost never publish the failures. Fedus considers these series of failures the most valuable type of data. The long-term goal is a superconductor that works at higher temperatures. Closer to revenue are materials for the semiconductor industry. The first named customer is a chipmaker with a heat problem.
On September 15, Periodic unveiled its model Neon: an existing trillion-parameter model fine-tuned with scientific literature and the lab's own data. For analyzing X-ray measurements, it beats GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 at lower cost, according to the company.
Prometheus is Bezos' artificial engineer
At Prometheus, Jeff Bezos is taking an operational role for the first time since stepping down as Amazon CEO in 2021. He runs the lab as co-CEO alongside Vik Bajaj, who led moonshot projects at Google X. About 150 employees come from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI, and Nvidia, according to GeekWire.
The bet is called "artificial general engineer." It has nothing to do with robotics, Bezos told CNBC. Prometheus is building tools that let engineers design physical objects much more easily: a fundamentally modernized version of CAD software. The long-term goal is software that takes an engine or a drug compound from concept to manufacturing. The data for that doesn't exist yet and has to be created, Bezos said, from physical laws and test results, for instance.
How Prometheus plans to get that data is hinted at by a second venture. According to the Wall Street Journal, Bezos held talks in March about a fund of roughly 100 billion dollars to buy and retool industrial companies in aerospace, chip manufacturing, and defense with AI. The biggest stores of engineering data sit in decades of CAD and simulation files at exactly these kinds of companies. Licensing that data is nearly impossible, since no company gives away its digital institutional knowledge willingly. Buying the companies could mean gaining access to their data too. That creates a possible strategic link: the fund wouldn't just be an industrial play but also a way to acquire training data for Prometheus' artificial engineer. This interpretation hasn't been confirmed.
From the reported rounds of 6.2 billion and twelve billion dollars, the total comes to more than 18 billion dollars. That makes Prometheus the most heavily funded lab in this issue, with no product and no published research.
Other labs with a similar goal
Lila Sciences in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is the closest relative of Periodic. In an "AI Science Factory," AI generates hypotheses, robots run the experiments, and the results feed back into training, across chemistry and biology. The edge is supposed to come from this loop, not from the robots. It doesn't run entirely without human oversight yet.
PhysicsX in London generates its data through simulation. A proprietary data factory has computed more than 20,000 aerodynamic simulations for car bodies. The more varied the data, the better the models handle new shapes, according to PhysicsX. Competitors with enough compute could replicate this.
Simile simulates humans instead of nature. The startup, founded by the Stanford researchers behind "Generative Agents," builds a behavioral model from interviews, purchase data, and controlled experiments with real people. Companies use it to test how customers react to prices or products. Investors valued Simile at two billion dollars in July. A general model can't get this kind of access to human behavior just by being smarter.
Enveda in Colorado is older than the current wave and applies the same recipe to natural products from plants. Its model PRISM learned from 1.2 billion chemical fingerprints. Half were measured in Enveda's own labs; the other half came from public sources.
The big players are building their own labs too
Anthropic is building its own biology lab in the San Francisco area where Claude will steer robots through experiments. The company acquired Coefficient Bio in April for about 400 million dollars. In October, Google described how its agents design, test, and learn from protein binders in its own wet lab. As early as August, DeepMind's Co-Scientist planned experiments for two-dimensional materials, close to Periodic's core business.
The specialists sometimes have a multi-year head start in building samples, labs, and partnerships. Whether that lead holds depends on how hard the infrastructure is to replicate and whether the data stays exclusive.
Bet 4: Compute is the bottleneck
Whether it's a world model, a robot, or an automated lab, everything runs on the same chips in the end. GPT-6 Astra was trained on more than 100,000 Nvidia GPUs, and according to Huang, 400,000 more are coming online. The fourth group asks how efficiently AI actually computes. The Transformer won in part because GPUs handle its math well. Anyone who wants to do things differently has two options: adapt the approach to existing chips or build different chips.
Inception refines text in parallel
Inception was founded by professors Stefano Ermon (Stanford), Aditya Grover (UCLA), and Volodymyr Kuleshov (Cornell). In 2019, Ermon and Yang Song introduced score-based generative models, a foundation for diffusion in today's image and video generators. ChatGPT writes token by token, each waiting for the one before it. Inception's Mercury models generate a rough draft of the entire answer and refine many parts at once, similar to how an image generator works a picture out of noise. That promises shorter wait times and lower costs. A Transformer still runs underneath. The founders aren't betting against the architecture; they're betting against how text is generated today.
Unlike most labs in this issue, Inception already sells via API. Mercury 3 shipped on October 19. According to Inception, it beats the smaller GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on eight of twelve benchmarks and outputs text four to eight times faster. With Mercury Decide, Inception also offers a decision model, competing directly with TypeSafe. It's not alone: Google showed Gemini Diffusion as early as May 2025. In May, Reuters reported that Microsoft was in acquisition talks, with Inception wanting more than a billion dollars.
Liquid AI builds powerful models for limited hardware
Liquid AI was founded by MIT researchers in 2023 and builds models that are lean from the ground up. They're designed for devices with limited memory and compute, anywhere a data center connection is too expensive, too slow, or unwanted. The LFM2 models replace the Transformer's compute-heavy attention mechanism in most blocks with cheaper operations that only consider a word's immediate neighborhood. The target device's memory and compute shape the model's structure, not the other way around, as the researchers describe in the LFM2 technical report.
On October 27, LFM3 followed as a new generation handling text, image, video, and audio, with open weights and designed for local deployment and specialization. Liquid has also offered a decision model called d1 since early October, now in several sizes, partly with open weights, and for images too. AMD led the 250 million dollar Series A. Since then, Liquid has been optimizing its models for AMD chips as well.
The models are now reaching cars. On November 5, the Wall Street Journal reported that Mercedes had begun rolling out Liquid's technologyin North America in October. Voice commands for navigation, music, or seat settings run directly in the vehicle. More complex requests still go to cloud models.
Ricursive Intelligence pursues self-improvement in silicon
Before founding Ricursive, Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini developed AlphaChip at Google, an AI method for arranging components on chips. Google used it across multiple TPU generations.
Ricursive's bet builds on that: AI designs better chips, which in turn power the next generation of AI. Conventional tools break a chip into dozens of blocks. Ricursive wants to optimize it as a whole. Long-term, models and chips should be co-designed, and a chip should take a week instead of months or years. Two months after launch, Ricursive announced a 300 million dollar Series A at a four billion valuation in January. No product.
On November 4, it released Ripple-65B Preview with open weights. Ricursive designed its architecture around Nvidia hardware to make training and running it more efficient. An internal version already powers its chip design platform. According to the company, Ripple ranks among the strongest US open models on coding tasks. Independent evaluations are still missing.
The competition is tough. Google has used AlphaChip for years. Nvidia optimizes circuits with PrefixRL. In late September, OpenAI teamed up with Synopsys. Along with Cadence and Siemens, Synopsys is one of the dominant chip design software providers. Their joint model GPT-Synopsys is supposed to operate Synopsys tools on its own and iteratively improve designs. Ricursive isn't just up against chip companies' internal R&D but against an alliance between a leading AI lab and a market leader in design software.
Unconventional AI wants to compute with oscillations
Unconventional wants to change the hardware AI runs on. Founder Naveen Rao has sold two AI companies before: Nervana to Intel and MosaicML to Databricks. He expects energy to become a hard limit for AI in about three years. Today's chips compute digitally, with billions of switching transistors. Unconventional wants to compute with analog coupled ring oscillators: oscillating circuits that influence each other until their rhythms align. This dynamic is supposed to take over part of the computation, merging memory and processing.
In June, the lab introduced Un-0 as a product demo of sorts, an open image generator built from up to 16,384 simulated oscillators. Its quality is a few years behind the state of the art. A first physical chip produced images in September.
A first rack system is planned within two years. Unconventional doesn't want to sell chips but offer compute capacity from its own systems. The company is also acquiring: on October 26, it announced the acquisition of NeuReality, an Israeli AI chip developer. The team will transfer. No price was disclosed.
Other labs with a similar goal
Extropic wants to change the physics of computing like Unconventional, just differently. Its circuits intentionally allow electronic noise in transistors and draw randomness from it for AI models. In the summer, Extropic said its Z1 chip is in fabrication, with first systems expected in 2027. The promised efficiency gains of several orders of magnitude come from simulations.
Normal Computing pursues a similar principle and earns money in the meantime with AI tools for chip design.
Cartesia, founded by the inventors of the Mamba architecture, replaces large parts of the compute-heavy attention mechanism like Liquid AI and sells the result mainly as models for spoken language.
Bet 5: Research itself becomes the product
The fifth group automates what their own researchers do: developing ideas, running experiments, analyzing results. How far a system has come can be roughly described in four stages:
Most publicly shown results sit at stage 2, with a few reaching stage 3 in limited form, at neolabs and big labs alike. Studies of automated research workflows continue to show a central role for human decisions. Automation goes furthest where a machine can verify the result itself: in mathematics.
Axiom Math builds proofs a machine can verify
Axiom wants to automate mathematical proofs. Carina Hong and Shubho Sengupta, previously at Meta, founded the company in 2025. Number theorist Ken Ono gave up his professorship to join.
The basic problem: a language model can write a proof that sounds convincing and is still wrong. Axiom gets around this by having its AI write in Lean, a programming language for mathematics where a proof checker verifies every step. If the proof passes, it's correct within the definitions and assumptions used. There's no way to bluff. Humans still need to check whether the original claim was correctly translated into Lean and whether any invalid extra assumptions crept in. If the translation is off, the machine flawlessly proves the wrong statement. Axiom describes this limitation itself.
On October 26, Axiom reported its biggest success so far: dozens of AI agents, under human guidance, translated the so-called "Enormous Theorem" into Lean in 24 days. The proof spans more than 10,000 pages across hundreds of papers from five decades. A single section of about 250 pages had previously taken a research team six years to formalize in the Coq proof system. The code is open on GitHub, about 43 million lines.
Along the way, the team found an error in a 1986 paper. According to mathematician Timothy Chow, the error was known to experts but apparently never publicly documented. The translation makes visible what only insiders knew.
Axiom doesn't plan to make money from math alone. The 200 million dollar Series A is meant to extend the method to software: AI writes code, and a proof shows it meets formally specified requirements. Tests check examples. A proof can cover all cases captured by the formal model.
Discovery Loop is Google funding its own departures
Discovery Loop wants to automate the entire cycle of scientific experiments, from proposal to analysis, thousands in parallel. Behind it are four of Google's best-known names: Jeff Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Quoc Le, and Oriol Vinyals, one of the leaders of Gemini development. The four left in early August, at the same time as a restructuring at Google. According to WIRED, the idea was only a few weeks old.
Google is a founding investor and cloud partner. Business Insider reported on talks for a seed round of about one billion dollars at ten billion in valuation. Weeks later, talks were already underway at about 50 billion. Machine learning research comes first, with Discovery Loop as its own first customer. Chip design, biology, and materials research are planned to follow. So far, there's a team, a mission, and an organization. For Google, it's a smart move: instead of losing four top people entirely, the company stays connected as investor and cloud provider.

Les sénateurs s’apprêtent à débuter plusieurs journées d’examen du budget de la Sécurité sociale. Retraites, prestations familiales, taxe sur le sucre ou encore cures thermales : le point sur les articles qui seront particulièrement débattus.
Présidentielle 2027 : avec la « Nouvelle France », Jean-Luc Mélenchon fait de l’écologie la clé de voûte de son programme
« La présidentielle, ce n’est pas la Star Academy de la politique. Ceux qui la voient comme un spectacle de claquettes finissent par être balayés, parce que les gens ne décident pas quel homme ou quelle femme sera le plus beau dans les habits de président, mais quelles idées ils veulent », martèle le député insoumis Aurélien Le Coq.
La formule résume la méthode de La France insoumise, faire du programme l’arme principale de sa campagne. Et le mouvement entend bien prendre les devants. À la veille d’un grand meeting au Bourget, en Seine-Saint-Denis, le mouvement publie l’intégralité de son programme pour 2027, avec la cinquième édition de L’Avenir en commun. Un ouvrage de 212 pages, vendu 4,90 euros en librairie, qui réunit 1 069 propositions, dont 238 nouvelles selon le décompte du mouvement.
Coordonné par les députés Clémence Guetté et Hadrien Clouet, le texte s’appuie sur plus de 24 000 contributions citoyennes, une trentaine d’auditions et le travail de groupes d’experts. « Les mesures proposées ne sont pas les intentions de quelques technocrates seuls dans un bureau », insiste Jean-Luc Mélenchon dans son introduction. « L’Avenir en commun est une mise en cohérence des programmes produits par la société elle-même. »
Mais cette nouvelle version n’est pas qu’un catalogue enrichi, elle marque aussi un tournant stratégique. L’écologie, longtemps cantonnée à la troisième partie, ouvre désormais l’ouvrage. Et la « Nouvelle France » prend peu à peu la place de l’« union populaire », le slogan de la campagne de 2022 et s’impose comme le nouveau fil conducteur du projet mélenchoniste.
L’écologie, nouvelle porte d’entrée du programme insoumis
C’est le changement le plus visible de cette cinquième édition, la bifurcation écologique et sociale devient la première des six grandes parties du programme. « Tout notre programme est structuré autour de la planification écologique, c’est le point de départ de notre action », explique à l’AFP Hadrien Clouet, coresponsable du projet. Sa collègue Clémence Guetté a défendu la même ligne ce vendredi sur France Inter, en insistant sur la prise en compte des « maladies écologiques ».
Dans le détail, les insoumis proposent d’inscrire dans la Constitution une « règle verte », qui empêcherait de prélever sur la nature davantage que ce qu’elle peut reconstituer, ainsi qu’une « règle bleue » reposant sur le même principe. Le mouvement entend également créer un conseil à la planification écologique, chargé notamment de superviser la relocalisation des productions essentielles. Autre mesure emblématique, déjà dévoilée avant l’été : la création d’« écorégions », un nouveau découpage territorial fondé sur les bassins versants, les massifs montagneux et les façades maritimes.
Sur le terrain énergétique, les insoumis maintiennent leur ambition de sortir du nucléaire et des énergies fossiles pour atteindre 100 % d’énergies renouvelables. Mais l’horizon est repoussé à 2060 au plus tard, contre 2050 dans le programme de 2022. Le texte fixe également un objectif de réduction de 65 % des émissions de gaz à effet de serre d’ici à 2033. La dimension internationale de cette bifurcation est aussi renforcée. LFI propose la création d’un tribunal international de justice climatique et environnementale, d’une organisation mondiale de l’environnement et d’un fonds destiné à indemniser les victimes de pollutions et à soutenir les lanceurs d’alerte.
Ce virage vert n’est pas sans arrière-pensée politique. En multipliant les propositions sur le sujet, les insoumis cherchent à occuper le terrain des écologistes, alors que le ralliement de leur appareil à une candidature Mélenchon reste incertain.
Des marqueurs historiques largement reconduits
Derrière cette nouvelle hiérarchie des priorités, les marqueurs historiques du programme insoumis demeurent largement préservés. Smic à 1 700 euros net, blocage des prix des produits de première nécessité, rétablissement de l’impôt de solidarité sur la fortune (ISF), taxation des très hauts patrimoines, « sécurité sociale intégrale », les principales propositions économiques et sociales des précédentes campagnes sont toujours là.
Sur les retraites, LFI promet d’abroger la réforme d’Emmanuel Macron. Elle prévoit d’abord un retour à 62 ans, avant de rétablir le droit à la retraite à 60 ans à taux plein après 40 annuités de cotisation. Un calendrier plus progressif que celui défendu en 2022.
Autre pilier du projet mélenchoniste, la VIe République reste elle aussi au programme, même si elle n’en est plus la porte d’entrée. Les insoumis veulent convoquer une assemblée constituante par référendum pour refonder les institutions. Ils proposent aussi d’accorder le droit de vote à 16 ans, de reconnaître le vote blanc et d’instaurer le vote obligatoire.
Le programme s’aventure aussi sur des terrains plus récents. Face à la montée en puissance de l’intelligence artificielle, LFI souhaite créer une autorité nationale chargée de délivrer des autorisations de mise sur le marché pour les systèmes présentant des risques élevés. Le mouvement entend également garantir un contrôle humain des décisions algorithmiques dans le monde du travail.
De nouveaux droits et un milliard d’euros contre le racisme
L’autre évolution de cette édition tient à l’élargissement des droits sociaux et sociétaux. Dans le prolongement de son travail sur la reconnaissance de l’amitié, Clémence Guetté porte plusieurs mesures pour mieux prendre en compte les liens familiaux et amicaux. Les insoumis proposent un congé de proche aidant et un congé de sept jours en cas de décès d’un proche, familial ou amical. Les insoumis proposent également de donner un statut légal au baptême civil et de créer un statut de famille monoparentale, ouvrant notamment droit à des réductions dans les transports.
Sur le terrain de la lutte contre les discriminations, le programme prévoit un plan d’un milliard d’euros contre « l’islamophobie, l’antisémitisme et toutes les formes de racisme ». Il envisage également, si nécessaire, un renforcement de la protection policière des lieux de culte. Un chapitre particulièrement étoffé, dans un contexte où le mouvement est régulièrement mis en cause sur ses positions et ses ambiguïtés dans la lutte contre l’antisémitisme.
À l’international, enfin, les insoumis restent fidèles à leur doctrine de non-alignement. Ils maintiennent leur volonté de sortir du commandement intégré de l’Otan et de mettre fin à « l’isolement occidental » de la France. Sur le conflit israélo-palestinien, le programme prévoit de faire appliquer le mandat d’arrêt visant Benyamin Netanyahou. S’il réaffirme la solution à deux États, il ouvre également la voie à la reconnaissance d’un État binational égalitaire.
La « Nouvelle France », ou l’ambition d’un nouveau récit politique
Au-delà des mesures, c’est aussi une bataille de mots et de représentations que Jean-Luc Mélenchon entend engager. À peine esquissée dans la campagne de 2022, la « Nouvelle France » irrigue désormais l’ensemble du programme. Elle succède à l’« union populaire », qui avait constitué la bannière de sa précédente candidature.
Dans son introduction, le candidat présente son projet comme une réponse à « la crise de la civilisation humaine » et oppose deux modèles : le « suprémacisme » et le « collectivisme ». « Le choix que nous allons faire en 2027, à l’occasion de l’élection présidentielle, est historique », écrit-il, avant de poser la question : « La France va-t-elle rejoindre le camp du suprémacisme mondial ? Ou bien va-t-elle puiser dans le meilleur de son passé pour étonner et entraîner le monde des peuples aux désirs pacifiques ? »
Avec cette « Nouvelle France », le leader insoumis cherche à dépasser le seul périmètre de son électorat. Le récit se veut fédérateur et inclusif, en s’adressant à l’ensemble du peuple français, au-delà des seuls sympathisants de LFI. Le changement de vocabulaire accompagne ainsi une ambition plus large, faire de la présidentielle non seulement un affrontement entre candidats, mais un choix de société. Pour Aurélien Le Coq, la force de Jean-Luc Mélenchon réside précisément dans la cohérence de son projet au fil des campagnes. « Jean-Luc Mélenchon est le candidat le plus politique et le plus cohérent. Il aura défendu le même programme à chaque élection. Cette clarté, cette constance et cette cohérence expliquent comment il est passé de 11 % en 2012 à 22 % en 2022 », défend le député du Nord. « Sa spécificité, et sa victoire en plus de dix ans, c’est d’avoir réussi à installer le programme comme un élément central et à fonder la campagne sur la conviction et sur le programme. »
Pour donner corps à ce projet, les insoumis se sont appuyés sur un réseau de 200 hauts fonctionnaires, surnommés « les Phrygiens ». Reste un point en suspens : le chiffrage complet ne sera dévoilé qu’au début de l’année 2027. Le candidat Insoumis a aussi dévoilé ce vendredi 6 novembre, à la veille d’un grand meeting au Bourget, une nouvelle affiche de campagne : Gergovie en fond, « Liberté, Égalité, Solidarité » en bleu, blanc, rouge.
Pour Jean-Luc Mélenchon, l’enjeu est désormais de transformer ce socle programmatique en récit de campagne, et de faire de la « Nouvelle France » le cadre politique de sa quatrième bataille présidentielle.

Au mois de septembre, le titre de la conférence de presse de rentrée du syndicat majoritaire chez les chefs d’établissement avait donné le ton : « Comment faire… avec rien ? » Le SNPDEN-UNSA alertait alors sur le niveau des enveloppes censées financer les projets culturels, l’accompagnement aux devoirs ou encore les remplacements ponctuels d’enseignants, sensiblement réduites au début de l’année scolaire 2026-2027 dans une large partie des collèges et lycées. Deux mois plus tard, la réponse tombe comme un couperet : « Il y a des dispositifs qu’on n’a plus les moyens de financer », expose Alex Berasategui, principal du collège Charles-Péguy, au Chesnay-Rocquencourt, et secrétaire départemental du syndicat dans les Yvelines.
Au sein de son établissement, l’enveloppe d’heures supplémentaires sur laquelle repose le dispositif « devoirs faits » est presque écoulée. « En septembre, le rectorat nous a versé une dotation correspondant à 15 % de nos moyens de l’année précédente, censée couvrir nos besoins jusqu’au mois de décembre », explique le principal. Outre qu’ils sont insuffisants pour assurer un tiers de l’année scolaire, tous ces crédits doivent, pour des raisons administratives, être engagés avant le samedi 7 novembre. A partir du lundi 9 novembre, les élèves ne pourront donc plus bénéficier de cet accompagnement, pourtant obligatoire en 6e depuis 2023. « Je ne sais pas si on touchera une nouvelle dotation. Donc, ça ne reprendra potentiellement pas et c’est une catastrophe », déplore Alex Berasategui.

Gravement touchées par des grenades policières lors de la manifestation du 17 octobre à Marseille, Suzanne, Laurie et Olive* resteront blessées à vie. Deux d'entre elles ont annoncé déposer plainte.
Elles ne se connaissaient pas avant le 17 octobre mais elles sont désormais liées par ce qu'elles ont vécu ce jour-là. Trois jeunes femmes de 21, 31 et 34 ans témoignent vendredi 6 novembre sur franceinfo. Toutes ont été très gravement blessées par des grenades de la police qui les ont mutilées aux pieds ou aux jambes en l'espace de trente minutes au même endroit à Marseille. Aucune n'est sûre de pouvoir remarcher normalement un jour. Deux d'entre elles vont déposer plainte dans les prochaines heures.
La nuit tombe près de la gare de Marseille quand Suzanne, Laurie et Olive* se retrouvent noyées sous les gaz lacrymogènes. Face à elles, un barrage de police, puis soudain des explosions, raconte Suzanne : "À l'endroit où j'étais, je ne pensais pas une seule seconde que je pouvais être atteinte par quoi que ce soit. On était assez loin. Au moment où je reçois l'explosif à mon pied, je suis juste sonnée, j'ai des acouphènes. Je suis vraiment comme suspendue. Je vois les gens qui me disent de venir vers eux, mais je n'avais même pas compris que j'étais blessée au pied."
"Une fois les acouphènes estompés, j'ai entendu les gens autour de moi et mes amis dire que j'avais un gros trou dans le pied. C'est là que j'ai compris que j'étais vraiment atteinte."
Suzane, victime d'une grenade tirée par la police
à franceinfo
"Ce sont des blessures de guerre"
Toutes les trois racontent cette sidération puis la découverte de leurs blessures : des trous béants jusqu'à 11 centimètres dans le pied ou dans la jambe et cette incertitude de pouvoir remarcher normalement un jour. "On est des cyborgs", résume Olive. "Ce sont des blessures de guerre, en fait. Si ça s'infecte, c'est l'amputation. Ce n'est pas pour être dramatique, mais c'est ce que les soldats de la seconde guerre mondiale avaient. Les gueules cassées, c'est nous", déclare Olive en riant.
Mais derrière ce rire se cache surtout une grande détresse psychologique, confie Laurie. "Je me rends compte qu'il y a un stress post-traumatique que je n'avais pas mesuré parce que j'habite dans le centre-ville de Marseille, pas très loin des points de départ des manifestations. J'entends les grenades tomber, j'entends des slogans. Il y a un stress post-traumatique existant que je ne peux pas nier. Il y a des nuits où je me réveille et j'ai du mal à croire que j'ai pris une grenade dans le corps. C'est quand même choquant", explique-t-elle.
"Je ne pensais pas, en tant que Française, bien que militante, vivre ça un jour dans ma vie."
Laurie, victime d'une grenade tirée par la police
à franceinfo
"C'est pénible de voir que c'est devenu un danger de manifester"
"C'est très angoissant cette situation. Il y a un basculement qui s'apparente à un règne de la terreur", estime Laurie. À tel point, ajoute Olive, qu'elle n'est pas sûre de retourner manifester un jour. "Ça fait aussi repenser l'engagement. Parce qu'on ne va pas se mentir, les gens qui manifestent, c'est quand même des gens qui sont concernés. Ils subissent beaucoup de choses dans leur vie et c'est pénible de voir que c'est devenu un danger de manifester. Donc comment on fait ?"
Laurie et Suzanne affirment avoir une peur panique pour leurs proches qui continuent de descendre dans la rue. Deux de ces trois jeunes femmes vont déposer plainte, surtout pour faire changer les choses. Saisir la justice n'était une évidence pour aucune des trois. Mais ce qui motive surtout Suzanne, c'est de se faire voir et de se compter pour avoir enfin un chiffre réaliste du nombre de manifestants blessés. "Il y a cette colère de ne pas voir les chiffres sortir des recensements de blessés. Qu'on ne sache pas combien on est, combien de personnes ça représente avec des blessures graves ou même plus légères. Il y a une grosse colère à plein de niveaux, mais surtout celle-là", s'indigne Suzanne.
Elles veulent aussi se battre aussi pour faire interdire ces armes qui, disent-elles, "peuvent tuer" et qui vont peut-être les laisser handicapées à vie. Ce combat lie désormais ces trois jeunes femmes qui s'écrivent tous les jours. C'est leur seul rayon de soleil, indiquent-elles, dans ce moment qui a fait basculer leur vie.

vidéo "Ce sont des conditions inacceptables" : au cœur d'un lycée vétuste à Montpellier, qui figure parmi les 200 établissements à rénover en priorité
- 
        
vidéo "J'ai besoin de plus d'argent" : dans les entreprises, patrons et salariés divisés sur une éventuelle hausse du Smic
- L'entrée d'un lycée incendiée à Lyon, huit personnes interpellées
