Budget 2027 : les points chauds lors des débats au Sénat du 9 au 17 novembre
Plus de 1 200 amendements ont été déposés sur le projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale (PLFSS) pour 2027 au Sénat. Ils seront débattus du 9 au 17 novembre, exception faite du 11 novembre et vraisemblablement du 15 novembre. Le vote solennel se tiendra le 18 novembre. Comme l’an dernier, les débats seront particulièrement scrutés, puisque l’Assemblée nationale n’a pu examiner le projet de loi en entier. Le rejet de la partie recettes en octobre a entraîné le rejet du texte dans son ensemble, et a empêché l’examen du volet dépenses.
En commission, le 4 novembre, les sénateurs de la majorité sénatoriale ont opéré des modifications limitées, mais certaines devraient faire parler d’elles.
De vifs débats en prévision sur les retraites
Un article devrait faire particulièrement faire débat. C’est l’article 35 qui propose de déroger à la règle selon laquelle les pensions de retraite doivent être indexées au 1er janvier sur l’inflation. Dans le texte déposé par le gouvernement, une revalorisation était prévue pour les pensions allant jusqu’à 1 260 euros. La commission des affaires sociales défendra un amendement pour porter le seuil à 1 500 euros. Ce filet de protection serait équivalent à celui l’an dernier où la commission avait soutenu un gel au-delà de 1 400 euros, soit un niveau proche du Smic net. Rappelant que la situation financière de la branche vieillesse reste « fragile », la rapporteure Marie-Do Aeschlimann veut également supprimer la possibilité offerte à l’exécutif de pouvoir procéder par décret en 2027 à une revalorisation plus importante des pensions, voire à une annulation du gel.
Les trois groupes de gauche et le groupe Union nationale pour les territoires (RN-UDR) veulent revenir sur cette désindexation partielle, avec des amendements de suppression. Au sein de la majorité sénatoriale, seul le sénateur LR Alain Houpert s’engage dans la même voie.
D’autres amendements visent à relever le seuil, comme celui de Marie-Claude Lermytte (Les Indépendants) à 1867 euros. La sénatrice de la Guadeloupe Solanges Nadille (RDPI) veut donner au gouvernement la possibilité d’une revalorisation différenciée dans les outre-mer, où le niveau des prix est plus fort que dans l’Hexagone. Les socialistes Victorin Lurel et Catherine Conconne veulent exclure les territoires ultramarins du gel des pensions.
À noter que les Indépendants veulent remplacer la revalorisation automatique des pensions de retraite en fonction de l’inflation par une décision annuelle du Parlement. Au moment des travaux en commission, le ministre du Travail Jean-Pierre Farandou avait évoqué la possibilité d’un amendement pour revenir sur le mécanisme d’indexation automatique à 100 % sur l’inflation.
La majorité sénatoriale veut revenir sur la suspension de la réforme des retraites
La commission des affaires sociales proposera le rétablissement de la réforme des retraites de 2023, suspendue l’an dernier. Un amendement du groupe Les Indépendants proposera le même type d’amendement, contre ce qu’ils estiment être une « grave erreur politique ».
Deux amendements, de Vincent Louault (Les Indépendants) et de Daniel Fargeot (Union centriste et indépendants) proposent également de supprimer le caractère automatique de la revalorisation des prestations sociales chaque année. Les écologistes porteront quant à eux un amendement ouvrant droit à un congé anticipatoire de retraite pour les personnes ayant atteint 62 ans et 42 annuités.
Quelle évolution pour le calcul des allègements généraux ?
L’article 7 devrait constituer l’un des premiers temps forts de la discussion. C’est l’une des dispositions les plus décriées par les organisations patronales. Il vise à prendre en compte des compléments de salaire, comme la participation, l’intéressement, ou encore l’abondement aux plans d’épargne entreprise, dans le calcul des allègements généraux. De nombreux amendements de suppression vont être défendus par des sénateurs issus des Républicains, de l’Union centriste, des Indépendants, ou encore du groupe Union nationale pour les territoires (RN-UDR). Les parlementaires dénoncent un renchérissement du coût du travail et craignent que ces dispositifs ne perdent en attractivité dans les entreprises.
La sénatrice centriste Brigitte Devésa proposera en outre de revenir sur le gel de la valeur du Smic dans le calcul des allègements généraux. À gauche, des amendements viseront à élargir l’assiette des cotisations. Les écologistes et les communistes veulent soumettre les primes de partage de la valeur à l’assiette des cotisations de sécurité sociale. Les premiers entendent également s’opposer dans le même article à la suppression du malus seniors, « seule sanction liée à l’obligation de négocier sur l’emploi des seniors ». Les socialistes essayeront d’étendre les cotisations au forfait social sur les sommes versées au titre de l’intéressement et de la prime de partage de la valeur dans les entreprises employant au moins 50 salariés.
L’extension de la taxe sucre va diviser au Sénat
Le débat sur les taxes comportementales est un classique des examens de projets de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale. Un article devrait donner lieu à des débats nourris : l’article 8. Il doit éteindre le champ de la taxe sur les boissons sucrées aux produits solides industriels transformés, contenant des additifs et contribuant le plus à la surconsommation de sucre.
La commission des affaires sociales veut conserver le dispositif, mais veut préciser les choses. Son amendement vise à exclure les denrées « non soumises à l’obligation d’étiquetage nutritionnel », et notamment celles « emballées sur le lieu de vente à la demande du consommateur ou préemballées en vue de leur vente immédiate ». De quoi exclure par exemple les chocolats vendus en ballotins. La commission veut aussi protéger les produits artisanaux et certains produits bénéficiant d’un signe officiel de qualité et d’origine français, comme le nougat de Montélimar.
On recense 9 amendements de suppression de l’article, qui cumulent au total une quarantaine de signataires, siégeant à droite au centre, chez les Indépendants, au RDSE ou encore au groupe UNT.
Le délai de carence d’un an imposé aux étrangers pour le bénéfice des prestations familiales
Le climat pourrait aussi se tendre sur l’article 37. Il vise à conditionner à une durée de résidence d’un an le bénéfice des prestations familiales (y compris la prestation d’accueil du jeune enfant) et les aides personnelles au logement (APL) pour les pour les ressortissants étrangers hors Union européenne.
Les trois groupes de gauche demandent sa suppression, mais également l’ancienne ministre Renaissance Brigitte Bourguignon, qui souligne que l’économie ne sera que de 62 millions d’euros par an. Les opposants à la mesure considèrent que cet article frappera avant « d’abord les enfants ».
Les sénateurs RN et UDR veulent porter la durée de résidence « stable et régulière » à 3 années, avant de pouvoir octroyer les prestations familiales. Vincent Louault (Horizons) propose deux années et demie, une durée supérieure de 6 mois à ce qui avait été voté dans une proposition de loi au Sénat en 2025. La sénatrice UDR Gaëlle Frontoni entend même proposer 5 ans, un seuil qui avait été censuré par le Conseil constitutionnel en 2024.
Protection des cures thermales
Question sensible au Sénat, la question de la prise en charge par la Sécurité sociale des cures thermales devrait cette année encore évoluer sensible. Le gouvernement veut faire passer par voie réglementaire le taux de prise en charge des cures thermales par la Sécurité sociale de 65 % à 15 %, pour une économie de 200 millions d’euros.
Le Sénat s’était déjà opposé à cette mesure lors de l’examen du PLFSS pour 2026. La commission des affaires sociales, soutenue par Jean-Marc Boyer (LR), une partie du groupe RDSE, plusieurs sénateurs socialistes, veut amender le projet de loi pour se prémunir contre un déremboursement mené sans étude. Celui-ci ne « pourra avoir lieu qu’après la publication par la Haute Autorité de santé d’un avis sur leur service médical rendu ».

BRUSSELS — Europe is once again watching the White House through gritted teeth.
An opaque Trump administration proposal for a new European-wide security arrangement with Russia has met skepticism from European capitals that fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin.
“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in reaction to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it ... Putin does not have a veto over European security.”

a55.texte:
Israel's Arab-led parties in spotlight after inconclusive election
KUFR QASI, Israel — In recent years many Palestinian citizens of Israel shunned elections, believing there was little to gain from participating in the politics of a state which, they say, regularly marginalizes their communities and oppresses their fellow Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
But last month, Palestinian Arabs in Israel came to the ballot boxes in record numbers, helping strip Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's most far-right government in Israel's history of its majority, and giving Arab-led parties the votes they needed to become a powerful force in Israeli politics.
"We blocked the government of Netanyahu from continuing," said Jamal Zahalka, chairman of the High Follow-Up Committee, the main umbrella body representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. "It's a historical achievement. I think our community found its strength."
Neither Netanyahu's coalition, nor his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot's center-right opposition, reached the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government. Arab-led parties won 19 out of 120 seats — enough to give them a critical role in the negotiations that will now determine who governs Israel at this turbulent moment in the country's history.
The election results strike at the heart of the decades-long questions about how Israel defines itself and the role of Palestinian Arabs in its society.
"The story still isn't over"
At a park in the Palestinian-majority town of Kufr Qasim two days after the election, hundreds of people gathered for the annual commemoration of residents gunned down in 1956 by Israeli border police on the opening day of the Suez Crisis in the violent early years of the state, when Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal.
"And today we stand here, 70 years later," the speaker told the large crowd from a podium: "And the story still isn't over."
The crowd at this event, mostly dressed in black — some wearing the keffiyeh, the black and white stitched scarf symbolizing Palestinian resistance — mourned not only their lost relatives all those years ago, but also the suffering of Palestinians now: the sharp rise in discrimination against their communities in Israel since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023; Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and left a population to survive amid the ruins of the enclave. And the actions of Netanyahu's extreme right-wing government in the occupied West Bank, where rights groups and the U.N. say it has armed and supported settlers as they force Palestinians from their homes and agricultural lands with unprecedented violence.
Worsening rights inside Israel was one reason, residents of Kufr Qasm told NPR, why so many Palestinian citizens in Israel went to the ballot boxes. "There is no freedom anymore," said Intisar Sarsur, 65, sitting with relatives beside an olive tree in the park in Kufr Qasim. " We are seeking for our basic rights as human beings."
"Everybody that I know participated in the elections. Not one person stayed home," Sarsur said. She and her family were sharing platters of mutabbaq, a sweet Palestinian layered pastry, and freshly pressed olive oil from this year's olive harvest — usually a joyous moment in the Palestinian calendar, that she said now felt bittersweet. This year the olive harvest for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank was marred by frequent attacks by Israeli settlers trying to disrupt this economically and culturally significant time of year.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, descendants of those who remained as the state of Israel was established in 1948 (when a majority of the prewar population was forcibly expelled or fled during the war) now make up about 20% of the population.
This election, Arab-led parties received a 64% increase in votes compared to the last elections, according to the Central Elections Committee. The gains they made have stirred anger, and even fear, among many on Israel's political right, who see them as a threat to the country's Jewish character.
Fear factor
Netanyahu and his allies made the large Arab turnout a rallying cry. On election day, Netanyahu posted a video calling it an "emergency." Itamar Ben Gvir, the far-right national security minister, filmed his own appeal at the entrance to Kufr Qasim: "If you want this country to remain Jewish and Zionist … then get out and vote!"
As results came in, Netanyahu's Likud party went further. It claimed Arab parties had "stolen" the election through bribery, threats and forgery, and later warned of a foreign takeover of the Knesset and the "Islamization of Israel." The party has made no evidence public. Police say they found no basis for the claims, and election officials say there was no widespread fraud. The head of the elections committee separately asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate suspected foreign funding of efforts to boost Arab turnout. But he and the attorney general say the vote was conducted properly and the results were not compromised.
The messaging by Netanyahu's bloc is widely seen as an attempt to prevent Eisenkot's center-right grouping from partnering with Arab parties — a reality that would give Eisenkot the majority he needs to form a government. But the sharp rise in anti-Arab sentiment since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed, has made an alliance with any Arab party potentially politically treacherous and could cause other Jewish right wing members of his bloc to split off in fury.
Eisenkot is not a natural ally for Arab parties either. A former military chief of staff whose son was killed fighting in Gaza, he served as an observer in Netanyahu's war cabinet early in the war. And he still cuts a hawkish figure. As a general, he is credited with formulating the "Dahiyeh doctrine," which he laid out in 2008: using "disproportionate force" against villages from which militants fire on Israel, which he called "not civilian villages" but "military bases." It is named after Beirut's southern suburbs, a Hezbollah stronghold that Israel largely decimated in heavy bombardment in 2006.
So Arab parties are divided on how to use the power they gained in this election. Ra'am, a socially conservative Islamist party, campaigned on joining a governing coalition and put a Jewish former police official second on its list. But for now the Joint List alliance that won 11 of the 19 Arab-led party seats in this election won't formally partner with Eisenkot. Its leaders have said they could back his government from the outside, but won't join it, citing Israel's ongoing war in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.
President Isaac Herzog has been consulting with parties over who they would support to try to form a coalition. He is expected to announce which candidate he'll give a mandate to next week, to try to form a coalition. That candidate will have 28 days and can ask for a further two-week extension. If he fails, another candidate is given only 28 days (without extension) to try to form a government. And if no one manages to form a coalition, there will be repeat elections next year.
In Kufr Qasim, as the readings and re-enactments of the 1956 killings unfurled on stage, Mansour Shaaban said he would vote again in an instant. Aged 33, this was the first election he had voted in. But now he said it's necessary to try to stop what he called the racism and oppression of Palestinians by Israel's extreme right. "There are Israelis we eat with and live alongside," Shaaban said. But Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir and other leaders in these last years he said "are making it impossible to co-exist," he said.
"Even if we don't succeed to create change this time," he said, now right-wing Israeli politicians know that Palestinian citizens of the country have found their voice.
Nuha Musleh contributed to this report.

La situation dans les grandes villes ukrainiennes s’est considérablement détériorée ces dernières semaines, notamment à Kiev, alors que l’armée russe accélère sa campagne de frappes sur les réseaux de production et de distribution d’électricité. Les centrales de production, lignes à haute tension et sous-stations sont prises pour cible de manière systématique : 238 frappes ayant touché des infrastructures énergétiques ont été recensées en octobre, selon ACLED.
Il s’agit d’un record depuis le début de l’invasion à grande échelle, en février 2022.
- Les centrales thermiques de Kiev ne produisent plus d’électricité, et la capitale dépend en majorité de trois centrales nucléaires situées à environ 300 kilomètres.
- Les longues distances parcourues par les lignes à haute tension pour transporter le courant depuis l’ouest et le sud du pays vers la capitale rendent la ville très vulnérable aux attaques, notamment car la portée des drones russes dépasse aujourd’hui les 1 000 kilomètres.
Les autorités de Kiev ont développé un réseau de petites centrales à gaz qui permettent d’assurer le fonctionnement de services essentiels – hôpitaux, une partie des stations de pompage d’eau, etc. –, mais celles-ci ne couvrent qu’une fraction des besoins de la ville.
Volodymyr Zelensky a décrit vendredi 6 novembre la situation énergétique à Kiev comme « la pire » du pays, évoquant des défis « très sérieux » 1. En plus des coupures d’électricité, des frappes russes ont privé mardi 3 novembre l’ensemble de la capitale d’eau pendant plus de 24 heures, selon les autorités municipales 2.
La situation pourrait davantage se dégrader étant donné l’asymétrie entre les capacités offensives russes et défensives ukrainiennes.
- La Russie serait en mesure de tirer entre 130 et 190 projectiles balistiques par mois cet hiver. Ces vecteurs sont trop rapides pour être interceptés par des drones ou d’autres moyens low cost, et nécessitent des intercepteurs 3.
- Or, l’Ukraine ne reçoit en moyenne que 12 missiles intercepteurs Patriot livrés par les États-Unis chaque mois, soit moins de 5 % du nombre nécessaire. Les intercepteurs européens, comme les missiles Aster du système SAMP/T, ne compensent qu’à la marge.
- En octobre, l’Ukraine n’a abattu que 11 des 150 missiles balistiques tirés par la Russie – soit environ 7 %.
L’hiver 2026-2027 sera vraisemblablement le plus difficile pour les Ukrainiens depuis le début de la guerre à grande échelle. La stratégie russe vise à rendre la capitale du pays inhabitable, en ciblant les infrastructures qui assurent le chauffage, l’éclairage ou l’approvisionnement en eau, afin de faire pression sur la population et d’user son moral.
- La Banque nationale d’Ukraine estime que l’intensification des bombardements russes sur les infrastructures du pays amputera la croissance ukrainienne de près de 2 points en 2026 4.
- Le PIB réel devrait se contracter de 0,4 % cette année, pour la première fois depuis 2022. Il avait enregistré une hausse de 1,8 % en 2025, 3,2 % en 2024 et 5,5 % en 2023.

Pedro Alliana has been sworn in as the new president of Paraguay, after a banking scandal led to the impeachment of his predecessor, Santiago Pena.
On Friday, Alliana, 52, took the oath of office to become the South American country’s 53rd president.
Previously, Alliana had served as vice president under Pena since the start of the latter’s term in 2023.
But Pena’s tenure came to an abrupt end earlier in the day, after 44 of Paraguay’s senators voted to remove him from office. One senator in the 45-member chamber abstained.
“I take my leave with gratitude, while fully acknowledging the anguish of those who are currently awaiting answers,” Pena wrote on social media on Friday afternoon.
The impeachment marked a rapid fall from power for Pena, a member of the long-governing Colorado Party. His departure coincides this week with the sudden collapse of a prominent lending institution, Ueno Bank.
Questions have arisen about whether the bank was properly regulated by government institutions, and whether Pena himself had conflicts of interest involving the bank.
After Pena’s impeachment, prosecutors ordered him placed under house arrest on suspicion of breach of trust and other crimes.
An arrest warrant was also issued for Carlos Carvallo, the former head of Paraguay’s central bank, which has been accused of failing in its oversight duties. Carvallo resigned earlier this week.
The scandal erupted early on Tuesday, when the central bank announced that Ueno had fallen below the legal standards for solvency, meaning it did not have enough collateral to cover its loans and other ventures.
It seized the lender, transferring its remaining assets to other banking institutions as a safeguard.
Millions of Ueno clients, however, abruptly lost access to their accounts and pension payments as a result of the crisis.
With roughly three million members, the bank counted nearly two-thirds of Paraguay’s adults among its customers.
The company had rocketed to prominence in recent years, consolidating in 2023 under the brand Ueno — sometimes stylised with lowercase letters as “ueno”. It had grown to be Paraguay’s fifth-largest bank by deposits, with $800m in public money fuelling its growth.
Prior to its collapse, Ueno claimed that more than a million Paraguayans had opened their first bank account with the firm.
In 2023, Pena was identified as a shareholder of Ueno’s parent company, though he claimed to have sold his shares in early 2025.
Following the collapse of the lender, Pena offered to step down, citing “the need to preserve our democratic institutions”.
But on Thursday, Paraguay’s Congress rejected his resignation and instead proceeded with his impeachment.
Pena’s conservative political movement, the Colorado Party, was among the groups in favour of the manoeuvre. The party has largely dominated Paraguayan politics since 1948.
“We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Pena, in order to restore the republic’s institutions,” Horacio Cartes, a former president and party leader, wrote in a statement.
Had Pena been allowed to resign, he would have retained the right of former presidents to become a member of the Senate, with legal protections from prosecution.
In Thursday’s hearing, the Chamber of Deputies voted 78 to zero to impeach Pena, allowing for the Senate to remove him from office the following day.
It declined, however, to open impeachment hearings against Alliana.
The newly inaugurated president began his political career as the governor of his home department, Neembucu, in Paraguay’s south, and he served nearly a decade in the Chamber of Deputies, including three years as its president.
Alliana assumes the leadership of Paraguay at a time when it is facing one of its most severe political and economic scandals in recent history.
Prosecutors have questioned whether Ueno was shielded from accountability due to its government connections. Some $355m in state pension funds were invested in the bank.
At least 27 people are facing criminal charges in relation to the scandal, including lead shareholder Miguel Vazquez.
Among the crimes being investigated are attempted fraud, breach of trust, misappropriation of funds and influence peddling.
Pena has signalled he plans to cooperate with the investigation, though he did not appear at the impeachment hearings personally on Friday, sending his lawyers in his stead.
“I do not wish for my presence to be a source of greater division or instability. It is my responsibility to place the country above my own personal fate,” he wrote in a statement.
Earlier in the day, however, he signalled displeasure with the fast pace of the Senate impeachment hearing, requesting an extension “to exercise [his] constitutional right to a defence, as the time currently allotted is clearly insufficient”.

responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of 
the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this 
growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 
11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when 
the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might 
reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate 
rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. 
Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In 
my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-
thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

1 Introduction
Artificial intelligence and automation may reshape the economy over the coming decades
(Trammell and Korinek, 2026). Such a transformation will require a great deal of capital: soft-
ware, data centers, robots, power plants, and much else. Van Nieuwerburgh (2026) estimates
that AI campuses alone will absorb 3.6% of GDP per year over 2025–2032, and much of that
capital will depreciate quickly, perhaps not physically but in economic terms.1 Who will save for
the machines?
The answer depends on two margins. The first margin is the task structure of production:
which tasks machines can perform, how productive they are at them, and how substitutable
tasks are for one another. In other words, the task structure governs the returns to accumulating
machines. The second margin is the supply of capital: how much households are willing to save
in response to the returns that machines generate. Capital supply determines how quickly the
economy exploits the existing technological opportunities. But the saving response is ambiguous
ex ante: expectations of higher future income encourage consumption today, while higher future
returns induce more saving.
I model capital supply with a representative household that saves optimally. In the long
run, the supply of capital is perfectly elastic: the return the household requires depends on
consumption growth, not on how much capital it holds. I compare my optimizing economy with
one in which the saving rate is fixed. Thus, I provide two polar cases for the saving response.
Other environments, such as models with household heterogeneity or financial frictions, generate
intermediate responses because their supply of capital has positive but finite elasticity.
Holding the path of automation and machine productivity fixed, the economy grows at 11.7%
a year when tasks are highly complementary and households save optimally, but at only 2.2%
if the saving rate remains at the calibrated 2025 rate of 23%. What looks like a technological
bottleneck under strong task complementarity can reflect insufficient capital accumulation.
The key to this result is that automation raises the capital share by moving tasks from labor
to machines. In comparison, ordinary technical progress makes labor and existing machines
better at the tasks they already perform and, in the Cobb–Douglas case, leaves the capital share
unchanged.2

share times the ratio of investment to capital income. If I take the evolution of the capital share

In my numerical exercises, the capital share rises from one-third to one under full automation,
whereas the ratio of investment to capital income moves only from 0.69 to about 0.55 while the
return climbs from 11% to 52%. In the U.S. data, too, the ratio has stayed between 0.50 and
0.78 since 1950. Thus, apart from its jump on impact, the model’s path for the ratio stays within
the historical range.
The model.The production side of the model is the task framework of Acemoglu and
Restrepo (2018, 2022): output is a CES aggregate of tasks and each task is performed by labor
or by machines, and the task structure collapses into a reduced-form production function in
capital and labor. With symmetric tasks and a Cobb–Douglas aggregator, Imas and Moll (2026)
show that this reduced form has two regimes, which they call cost parity and capital cheaper.
I extend their result: if machines have the same comparative advantage in every task they can
perform, the two regimes survive for any elasticity of substitution across tasks, even when labor
and machines improve at different rates and tasks differ in productivity and weight. When the
comparative advantage of machines differs across tasks, the two regimes merge into one.
With a constant, limited automatable set and constant machine productivity, the model be-
haves like the neoclassical growth model with a Cobb–Douglas production function: the economy
has a balanced growth path (BGP), and local convergence to it is faster the stronger the com-
plementarity across tasks. With a fixed, limited automatable set but continuously improving
machine productivity andσ <1, there is no fixed BGP. Instead, the economy remains close to
the BGP implied by current machine productivity, but with the gap shrinking over time. Along
the way, the capital share and the saving rate fall toward zero: better machines make capital
cheap, not dominant. Under full automation, production becomes linear in capital, as in Ace-
moglu and Restrepo (2018); with common comparative advantage, the model takes the form of
an AK economy with a labor-income endowment and a closed-form solution. The saving rate
converges to the IES, exactly so when machines keep improving and within a few points of the
IES when they do not.

Quantitative results.I calibrate the model to the U.S. economy and compute the tran-
sition to full automation, with every task becoming automatable between 2025 and 2045. In
my benchmark calibration, the optimizing household eventually saves more than half of output.
With a unit elasticity of substitution across tasks,σ= 1, and the benchmark IES of one-half,
households save 15% of output on impact and 54% in the limit; with log utility, the numbers are
52% and 93%; with an IES of one-third, 10% and 41%. A fixed saving rate, by contrast, delivers
a growth boom only above a threshold that rises with task complementarity: 23% clears it with
σ= 1, where growth in 2045 is then 6.5% instead of 22%, but not withσ= 0.2.
While endogenous saving fuels the growth boom,σshapes the transition. Withσ= 1, the
prospect of a richer future dominates and consumption jumps 10% when the automation path
becomes known. Withσ= 0.2, the higher return to saving dominates and consumption falls 9%.
But output rises far above its no-automation trend in both cases: by 2045 it is about sixteen
times trend withσ= 1 and five times trend withσ= 0.2. Wages, however, remain between a
quarter and a half of trend under common comparative advantage, because under full automation
labor cannot earn more than the cost of the machines that replace labor.
Under partial automation, the task structure determines how long the growth boom lasts.
With 85% of the tasks labor performs today becoming automatable, the economy resembles the
fully automated one until about 2040. What happens after that depends onσ. Withσ= 1, the
economy behaves like an AK economy for a century, and growth remains above 12% in 2065.
Withσ= 0.2, growth returns to near 2% by 2065, and the saving rate falls back toward its
initial level, reaching 32% in 2065 and 29% on the new BGP.
Withσ= 0.2, the tasks that remain with labor eventually become the bottleneck. Their
scarcity rents are large: after falling to little more than a quarter of trend in 2040, the wage
rises to nine times trend. For long-run labor income, whether the last tasks are automated is
therefore the key distinction. This is Ricardo’s rent in a new dress: tasks that only labor can
perform become a factor in fixed supply (Ricardo, 1817). Full automation escapes this logic
because the interest rate remains pinned down by machine productivity net of depreciation, so
the gains accrue to capital.
The full-automation wage result depends on machines having a common comparative advan-
tage. When comparative advantage differs across tasks, machines take the tasks they do best
first; as they move to worse tasks, the return to capital falls, while labor retreats to the tasks
where machines perform worst and earns scarcity rents even under full automation. The growth
boom barely changes, but the wage recovers. Withσ= 0.2, the wage bottoms between 0.43 and
0.63 of trend instead of 0.28, and with enough dispersion it eventually returns to trend. Common
comparative advantage is, thus, a knife-edge for the wage, but not for saving or growth.
4
In summary: under full automation, the task structure sets the long-run return to capital
for allσ, and capital supply determines how fast the economy grows; under partial automation,
preferences pin the long-run interest rate, and the task structure determines whether the gains
accrue to capital or labor. Along the transition, capital supply shapes the speed of the growth
boom and the task structure shapes the path of wages.
Welfare and distribution.The welfare gains from automation are large. To be as well off
without automation, the representative household’s consumption would need to grow at about
5% to 10.5% a year, rather than the 1.62% in the pre-automation BGP. Much of that gain comes
from optimal saving. Withσ= 0.2, automation is equivalent to a 109% increase in consumption
at every date with optimal saving, but only 26% when the saving rate remains at 23%.
These welfare gains accrue to the representative household as a whole, even though under
full automation its labor income falls to half of trend or less. To study distribution, I split the
household into two groups: hand-to-mouth households, which consume their labor income and
hold no assets, and owners, who hold all the capital and save optimally. Under full automation,
this split leaves the long run unchanged because labor income vanishes relative to output, and it
slows the transition only slightly. But the gains are no longer shared: hand-to-mouth households
lose the equivalent of 40% to 65% of their consumption, while owners gain even more than the
representative household.
Since output grows much faster than the wage falls relative to trend, the transfer required to
keep labor income on trend is small relative to output: it peaks at 4% of GDP withσ= 1 and
20% withσ= 0.2, and it is below 4% by 2055 in both cases. Furthermore, financing this transfer
with a tax on capital income has modest growth costs: growth falls by at most 1.1 percentage
points withσ= 1 and 3.3 points withσ= 0.2, and not at all in the long run.
Prices and wealth.I also look at asset prices. When the automation path starts, the
short rate does not move: the stock of machines is given. But a ten-year bond competes with
the machines that will be built over the next ten years, and those machines will earn 25% to
46%. So the ten-year real yield jumps on impact from 5.1% to 13.6% withσ= 1 and to 9.3%
withσ= 0.2, and the thirty-year yield to 33.0% and 19.6%.
The same high rates cut the value of the labor force by two-thirds on impact: the start of
automation does to human wealth what a permanent rate hike does to a long bond. The stock
market, however, does not move on impact, because market value equals the capital stock and
machines earn no rents. The boom in the market is a boom in quantities: under full automation,
market value grows at 10% to 16% a year in 2035, while the price-earnings ratio falls from 20 to
between 2 and 4 by 2045.

Related literature.The production side of my model traces back to Zeira (1998): ma-
chines replace labor task by task. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018) built the modern task frame-
work around this idea and already embedded it in a dynamic model with representative-household
saving and endogenous capital accumulation. They characterize balanced growth paths, includ-
ing full automation, and also study the adjustment of capital when automation runs ahead of
the creation of new tasks. I take the paths of automation as given and focus on how the saving
response changes the transition along those paths. Full automation also appears in Aghion et al.
(2019), where Baumol’s cost disease keeps growth bounded as the automated share approaches
one. Jones and Tonetti (2026) calibrateσ= 0.2 and find a slow acceleration from AI. I show
that, with optimal saving, that slow acceleration becomes double-digit growth.
Imas and Moll (2026) put this technology into a Solow model and compute a transition
with growth above 10% within a decade and a labor share that converges to zero. I keep their
automation path and two regimes, extending the latter toσ̸= 1, but let the household choose
saving optimally along the transition. Imas and Moll note that under full automation a log-
utility household would save 1−0.047/Rof output, the limit in Proposition 17; my focus is on
how this endogenous saving response interacts with the task structure throughout the transition.
Farboodi et al. (2026) obtain explosive growth from the interaction of endogenous data and
capital accumulation: data raises machine productivity and expands the automation frontier,
so even a fixed positive saving rate can generate a growth explosion. While their mechanism
operates through endogenous technological change, I take the automation path as given.
The literature models saving in different ways. In overlapping-generations models, saving
comes out of wages, so automation that depresses wages chokes off investment: Sachs and Kot-
likoff (2012) and Benzell et al. (2015) get immiseration, and Gasteiger and Prettner (2022) show
that an AK production side may fail to deliver long-run growth. Berg et al. (2018) let only
capitalists and skilled labor save and find real wages falling for generations. An infinitely lived
household is the opposite benchmark: since labor and capital income are fungible, the saving rate
can ultimately rise sharply as capital income expands (Propositions 10 and 17). Moll et al. (2022)
are closest to my emphasis on capital supply. Their supply of capital slopes upward, so automa-
tion raises the return to wealth, by a margin that grows with the capital share, and benefits those
who already own it. They contrast this case with the perfectly elastic representative-household
benchmark. In their growing economy, however, long-run growth is driven by exogenous pro-
ductivity growth; here, once automation becomes sufficiently extensive, the saving response can

change the growth rate itself.
Optimal saving when machines replace labor is much older than the current debate over AI.
Steigum (2011) obtains endogenous growth without scale effects when robot capital is a close
substitute for labor, as in my case with ˆ︁ψk = 0, and Prettner (2019) gets perpetual growth
without technological progress in a Solow model with automation capital. Erdil et al. (2025)
solve numerically a planner’s problem in which compute drives automation.
Korinek and Suh (2024) show that wages collapse once machines can perform every task
humans can, and Restrepo (2026) gives the sharpest statement of the limit: with artificial
general intelligence, wages converge to the cost of the compute that reproduces human work. I
obtain the same limit with endogenous saving and add the price of the future stream of wages.
Korinek et al. (2026) also obtain rapid growth and a falling labor share, but do not endogenize
saving or the interest rate. Chow et al. (2025) use long rates to infer market expectations of
transformative AI, while Trammell and Korinek (2026) emphasize that saving may rise or fall
with interest rates.

leave the growth boom intact: adjustment costs take four to seven points off limit growth with
σ= 1 and one to three withσ= 0.2.
11 Conclusion
I have asked how much the macroeconomic consequences of automation depend on the capital
supplied to exploit it. The answer changes how we should interpret technological bottlenecks to
AI-driven growth. Strong complementarity across tasks can leave growth near its historical rate
when saving remains fixed and still produce double-digit growth when households save optimally.
What looks like a technological bottleneck can therefore be a capital-supply bottleneck: the task
structure determines the returns available from accumulating machines, while capital supply
determines how much of that opportunity the economy exploits.
The distinction between a technological and a capital-supply bottleneck has observable im-
plications. First, the saving rate should track the capital share. Investment as a share of capital
income barely moves in my simulations, from 0.69 to about 0.55, so if the capital share climbs,
investment should climb with it. If investment stays at a fifth of GDP while the capital share
rises, the plow-back ratio must fall sharply, unlike along the optimizing paths of Section 7, and
the Solow benchmark describes the world better. Second, the early years are informative about
σ. Withσ= 1, the start of automation brings a consumption boom, higher wages, and a dip in
saving. Withσ= 0.2, consumption falls at once, saving jumps, and the wage is below trend by
2032. Finally, long real yields should jump on impact while the short rate stays put. Holding
the automation path fixed, the size of the jump is informative about the saving response: with
a fixed saving rate andσ= 0.2, there is no growth boom and long yields barely move. On the
other hand, the data will not tell us for decades whether the last tasks will be automated and
whether the interest rate will return toρ+γg.
The main thrust of my results rests on a sufficiently elastic supply of capital, and many
mechanisms can cap that elasticity: heterogeneous agents, financial frictions, and limited phys-
ical resources. Of all of them, I am intrigued by heterogeneous agents. The hand-to-mouth
households of Section 8.2 are a first step, with the ownership of capital fixed; a model in which
it moves is the natural next step. Other forms of capital deserve attention too, housing above
all. Beachfront lots in Montecito will be the same with or without automation. If automation
multiplies output by a factor of 100, I wonder what those lots will fetch in 2126.
And then there is political economy, probably the most important omission of my analysis.
A wage that falls to a quarter of trend for two decades is unlikely to be greeted with unremitting
merriment by the median voter. The equilibrium path studied here therefore describes what
the technology and the supply of capital permit, not necessarily what political institutions will
allow.

A historic runoff election took place in Brazil last month. Lula da Silva defeated the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro by nearly 4.4 million votes. Flávio left the country and arrived in the USA seeking asylum, despite a judicially imposed travel ban on leaving Brazil and the suspension of his passport in connection with an investigation into alleged corruption and money laundering. His father, Jair Bolsonaro, was convicted of attempting a coup. In the original version of a letter addressed to “the Brazilian people and the international community”, Flávio declared himself the elected President.
The outcome of this election, together with Flávio’s early attempts and those of some of his supporters to cast doubt on the result, provides an opportunity to take stock of the resilience of Brazilian democracy and the pressures it continues to face. This electoral period has made clear that the future of Brazilian democracy will depend heavily on two things. First, on social mobilization and engagement – as the unprecedentedly intense coordinated digital mobilization of the pro-Lula movement showed. Second, on curbing potentially abusive powers of digital platforms – such as those apparently exercised by Meta against Lula and pro-Bolsonaro. Yet I believe there is a further, institutional layer to this discussion that should not be overlooked: Tomorrow’s Brazilian democracy urgently needs stronger institutions and the strategic reduction of excessive decision-making powers concentrated in individual actors.
Mapping Individual Powers in Brazil
In Brazil, far too few people can make far too many decisions. Across the central institutions of the Brazilian state, there are opportunities to reduce these powers, which carry significant risks of abuse — risks that have become particularly visible over the past decade. This applies not only to the Presidency of the Republic but also to the Federal Supreme Court (STF), the National Congress, and the Office of the Prosecutor-General of the Republic, to name just a few. The prospects for Brazilian democracy will be considerably more uncertain if these entrenched forms of institutional individualization are not addressed.
The Presidency of the Republic
Within the Brazilian state, the institution currently in the spotlight is the Presidency of the Republic. Among the many controversies surrounding its individualized powers, one is particularly timely: the appointment of justices to the STF, a power vested exclusively in the President (Articles 84, XIV, and 101, sole par., of the Brazilian Constitution).
Two ways can mitigate the problems arising from this individualized appointment power. As I have discussed elsewhere, the first option is to reduce politicagem: to end the practice of appointing persons suspected of benefiting from personal favoritism with the President or of lacking the qualifications required for the position, in accordance with the criteria established by Article 101 of the Constitution.
The second option is a structural approach, one Lula has already considered. The model for selecting STF justices is not constitutionally immutable, nor does it need to be so heavily centered on the President. Entrenched eternity clauses may impose limits on appointment models (in particular, Article 60, par. 4, III of the Brazilian Constitution). There would nevertheless appear to be room for formal changes to the appointment process. Even without amending the Constitution, it is possible to develop constitutionally acceptable ways to informally change how candidates for the STF are proposed. In this respect, the possibility of establishing institutional councils to participate in the selection process, as Lula has proposed, may offer a starting point. Any such arrangement would, of course, need to preserve the role of the Federal Senate in approving appointments.
The Federal Supreme Court (STF) 
Distrust of the STF has reached record levels in recent months. This distrust has been fueled by accumulating non-collegial practices within the Court, which reached a peak in a disastrous plenary session held shortly before the first round of the elections. The session was called by the Chief Justice after three different Justices had issued conflicting monocratic decisions surrounding a major corruption scandal. Two of these Justices, in particular, ordered the Federal Police to investigate the other respective Justice. As a result, the broadcast session became a public display of virulent personal disputes that worryingly overshadowed the very first round of the elections.
Against this background, the need to reform the STF has become something of a national consensus. The Court’s problem of structural individualization, especially as manifested in its lack of collegiality, has persisted for far too long. Its legitimacy has suffered from the extensive use of powers that allow Justices to issue monocratic decisions with far-reaching structural effects, to postpone collective voting through pedidos de vista, and, in the case of the Chief Justice, to exercise extensive individual agenda-setting powers – to name just a few.
The problem, moreover, does not end with the Court’s formal decision-making powers. Most STF Justices have been involved in publicly reported activities that have raised serious questions about their (appearance of) impartiality. This has intensified the discussion about abuses of individual powers outside the Court, including serious suspicions concerning influence-peddling through recurrent non-transparent meetings between Justices and selected groups of lobbyists, entrepreneurs, and politicians, as well as allegations of unethical or even illegal financial benefits associated with their activities outside the Court.
The core of the various reform proposals is, and should be, one and the same: to strengthen the STF as an institution by reducing the individualized powers of its Justices, both inside and outside the Court. The precise form of such reform will require further maturation, but it should be guided by one central objective: to maximize, both in fact and in appearance, the practice of the STF as a genuinely impartial and collegial court, without undermining the functional conditions necessary for the exercise of its constitutional competences.
This could be pursued through measures such as strategically reducing the scope for Justices to issue monocratic decisions (such as those in abstract judicial review); adopting rules governing Justices’ conduct before, during and after their time in office (for example, through a Code of Ethics); and subjecting the Chief Justice’s agenda-setting powers to collective control, or at least the possibility of review by the Court as a whole.
Brazilian democracy’s tomorrow will need a well-functioning, impartial, independent, and genuinely collegial STF. The pressure for reform is increasing, and an unreformed Court may not be able to sustain its institutional and sociological legitimacy for much longer.
A Brief Digression: The Extended Voting Period in the Brazilian Elections
A brief observation is warranted here. The power of monocratic decision-making was felt particularly strongly during the second round of the elections, when a decision was issued to extend the voting period. This episode provides a useful opportunity to clarify that not all exercises of monocratic power should be restricted in the same way. Measures adopted under conditions of extreme urgency raise a different set of considerations.
After what amounted to a “non-decision” by TSE President Justice Kássio Nunes Marques, and following requests from both Lula’s and Flávio’s parties to extend the voting period, STF Justice Cristiano Zanin monocratically decided to extend voting hours throughout Brazil by two hours. Zanin could only make this decision less than 30 minutes before voting was due to end, when voting machines were already being closed across the country. As Zanin’s decision was published shortly after the official end of the voting period (5 pm), most machines had already been closed before the officials responsible for them learned of Zanin’s decision, and they could not be reopened — as Zanin and Nunes Marques themselves subsequently confirmed.
Shortly after the elections, it became mathematically evident that the election result would not have been different, even if all machines had remained open. But regardless of the decision’s impact, because it established the same conditions nationwide, its urgency both substantiated its equal application and justified its individual character. The extreme urgency, combined with the fact that both opposing parties had requested an extension, justified the exceptional adoption of a monocratic decision. All polling stations across the country were subjected to the same situational and urgent measure of remaining open. There was no discrimination, and the measure did not produce the worst possible outcome under the given circumstances. To paraphrase Aury Lopes Jr., in many situations, a suboptimal decision is better than no decision at all.
But the very special circumstances of Zanin’s decision should not obscure the broader picture: abuses involving monocratic decisions and Justices’ conduct must urgently be curtailed.
The National Congress
There are at least two areas in which Brazil’s democracy tomorrow depends on curbing individualized power within the National Congress.
The first concerns the powers of the presidents of the Chamber of Deputies and the Federal Senate. The main problem is the lack of adequate checks and balances, as well as procedural rights that enable parliamentary minorities to challenge or counterbalance these powers. These powers include extensive discretion over agenda-setting, initiating (or not) impeachment procedures, shelving requests, and various procedural maneuvers.
The second concerns parliamentary budget amendments. It is not democratically justifiable for one-fifth of the federal government’s discretionary budget to be controlled through parliamentarians’ individual allocation of resources. The National Congress shares responsibility for formulating the public budget and overseeing its implementation, but it should do so as a collective body, not as a collection of individual islands.
Representative democracy rests on political contestation, deliberation, and the formation of collective decisions. Excessive individualized powers within parliament undermine democratic conditions by detaching them from broader collective priorities and accountability.
The Prosecutor-General of the Republic
Last but not least, Conrado Hübner Mendes has explored how the Prosecutor-General of the Republic holds what he describes as the most powerful unreviewable power in the Brazilian Republic: the sovereign authority to exercise or refrain from exercising the office’s exclusive powers. These include decisions on whether to investigate or prosecute the country’s leading political figures. Mendes denounced that the abuse of this power can bring the Republic to a standstill, as it did during Jair Bolsonaro’s government.
Reform could involve both formal and informal changes to the internal structures within the Public Prosecution Service that hold the Prosecutor-General accountable. The aim should be to ensure that decisions of such consequence do not depend excessively on the discretion of a single officeholder, while preserving the institutional independence necessary for the exercise of prosecutorial functions.
Brazilian Democracy Lives 
The continued resilience of Brazil’s democracy will depend in part on social mobilization and engagement (including digital engagement), as well as on the capacity to investigate and constrain the partisan political influence of media companies and the predatory interests of foreign actors. But social mobilization alone is unlikely to secure Brazil’s democratic future. That future will also depend on institutional restructuring and the strategic reduction of individualized decision-making powers to contain risks to democracy and the rule of law.
The strategic reduction of individual powers means preventing attacks on, and distrust of, democracy from originating in the stroke of a single person’s pen. It means building institutions that can withstand the choices, interests, and abuses of individual officeholders.

As the European Union intensifies efforts to restrict Moscow’s access to international finance, attention is shifting from successive sanctions packages to the networks that allow Russian money, technology and energy exports to cross borders despite existing restrictions.
The European Commission convened senior officials from EU member states and international partners in Brussels on 5th November to examine weaknesses in the enforcement of sanctions against Russia. The discussions covered cryptocurrency transactions, foreign payment networks, military procurement and the maritime infrastructure supporting Russian oil exports.
The meeting reflects a problem that has become increasingly important as Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine approaches its fifth anniversary: imposing economic restrictions is considerably easier than preventing determined businesses, financial intermediaries and trading networks from circumventing them.
The Commission’s tenth High-Level Group on Union Restrictive Measures, chaired by Financial Services Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque, brought together national authorities responsible for implementing European sanctions.
A separate forum, convened by EU Sanctions Envoy David O’Sullivan, included representatives from Britain, the United States, Japan, Canada and other international partners, alongside Ukraine.
According to the European Commission’s announcement, discussions focused on strengthening enforcement and identifying emerging methods of sanctions circumvention.
The limits of successive sanctions packages
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, the EU has progressively restricted access to European financial markets, advanced technologies, industrial equipment and revenue from energy exports.
The 21st sanctions package, adopted on 23rd July 2026, extended transaction prohibitions to another 33 Russian financial institutions and four banks in third countries.
It also targeted 14 cryptocurrency service platforms operating outside the EU and introduced additional restrictions on entities involved in Russia’s military-industrial supply chains.
Yet the increasingly extensive legislation creates a corresponding enforcement challenge.
A financial transaction prohibited through a Russian bank may be redirected through an intermediary elsewhere. Restricted industrial components can pass through multiple jurisdictions before reaching their ultimate destination. Oil shipments can involve complex ownership arrangements, changing vessel registrations and service providers operating beyond European territory.
None of these methods necessarily proves illegal conduct by every intermediary involved. Establishing violations requires evidence concerning the transaction, the applicable rules and the parties’ knowledge or responsibilities.
The central question for European regulators is therefore whether they can trace the commercial relationships underlying prohibited activity.
Cryptocurrency and alternative payment systems
Financial circumvention featured prominently in Thursday’s discussions.
Restrictions on conventional banking have encouraged scrutiny of alternative payment arrangements, including crypto-assets and networks connecting Russian businesses with intermediaries in third countries.
The July sanctions package introduced a mechanism allowing the EU to prohibit transactions with foreign cryptocurrency providers used to facilitate Russian sanctions evasion.
This represents an extension of European financial restrictions beyond institutions physically established inside the Union.
Nevertheless, the effectiveness of such measures depends on cooperation with countries whose regulatory priorities may differ from those of Brussels.
European authorities must also distinguish legitimate international commerce from transactions designed to conceal Russian beneficiaries or prohibited end users.
For compliance departments in banks and multinational companies, this creates additional requirements to investigate ownership structures, payment routes and the actual recipients of goods and services.
Russia’s shadow fleet remains a central concern
The maritime sector presents another enforcement challenge.
Russia has continued exporting oil using tankers operating through complicated ownership and insurance arrangements, including vessels widely described as belonging to its shadow fleet.
The July package added 41 vessels to European restrictions, bringing the total number affected by the relevant measures to more than 670.
Brussels has also expanded attention to the services that make such operations possible, including bunkering, crewing and support arrangements.
The issue extends beyond sanctions compliance. European governments have raised concerns about ageing vessels, uncertain insurance coverage, maritime accidents and the security of critical undersea infrastructure.
However, restricting a vessel’s access to European ports does not automatically prevent it from transporting oil between countries outside the EU.
Enforcement consequently requires cooperation with flag states, insurers, shipping companies and authorities in major trading centres.
An economic contest measured over years
The Commission maintains that sanctions have contributed to Russia’s economic difficulties, citing a decline in annual growth from 4.9 per cent in 2024 to 1 per cent in 2025.
Nevertheless, the effectiveness of sanctions cannot be assessed through economic growth alone.
Russia’s capacity to finance military production depends on government expenditure, export revenues, access to imported components and its ability to redirect resources towards defence.
Elevated international oil prices, particularly amid instability in the Middle East, complicate European efforts to reduce Moscow’s revenue.
This makes the enforcement of existing restrictions an increasingly important element of EU policy.
For Brussels, the immediate objective is not simply to announce further prohibitions. It is to determine whether prohibited goods, money and services can still reach their intended destinations through alternative channels.
The outcome will depend less on the number of additional names entered on sanctions lists than on whether European authorities and their international partners can make circumvention more difficult, more expensive and more readily detectable.

On Thursday 5 November at a meeting of national and G7 coordinators responsible for monitoring sanctions against third countries, European Commissioner for Financial Services Maria Luís Albuquerque announced the creation of an internal European Commission office to monitor European Union sanctions across the entire economic lifecycle.
The office will focus on EU sanctions on third countries, particularly Russia. Its remit will extend “from policy design to outreach implementation, and of course circumvention”, Commission spokesperson for financial services Siobhan McGarry confirmed on Friday 6 November. The aim is to “give member states quicker access to guidance, data sharing, [and] economic and technical analysis, and ensure that we are harmonising the implementation and enforcement of our sanctions so that we can continue to maximise their impact on Russia itself”, she added.
Cryptocurrencies. Ms Albuquerque also announced the creation of a working group on sanctions targeting the cryptocurrency market, as these financial instruments are used to circumvent EU sanctions. The General Court of the European Union has annulled one part of the sanctions imposed on the Russian Maritime Register of Shipping. The rest of the restrictions stay in place.
A Russian state-owned ship inspector has beaten the European Union in court, but only just. The Russian Maritime Register of Shipping, or RMRS, is a non-profit entity that is 100 per cent owned by the Russian state. It brought an action for annulment in Case T-535/24 against measures the EU adopted in response to the war in Ukraine.
The sanctions followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The Council of the EU extended its regime to RMRS. It placed the body on lists carrying investment bans and transaction prohibitions. It also banned ships certified by RMRS from entering EU ports and locks.
The Council also withdrew the EU-level recognition of RMRS as an authorised ship-inspection and certification organisation. It required member states to revoke the body’s authorisations. That last measure is the one the court has now struck down.
A narrow victory
The court annulled the provision requiring the withdrawal of recognition. It found that the measure went too far or lacked proper legal justification under the EU’s rules on ship inspection, set out in Regulation 391/2009. The Council cannot use this tool to disqualify RMRS as a recognised safety organisation.
RMRS will not feel the benefit soon. The court ordered that the effects of the annulled provision stay in force for no more than two months and ten days from the date of judgment. That gives the Council a window of 70 days.
The Council can use that time to rewrite the text or to appeal to the European Court of Justice (ECJ). Until the period expires, the practical ban on RMRS’s recognition remains. If the Council appeals, the annulment is frozen until the ECJ rules. The sanction then stays active throughout.
Everything else survives. The court dismissed the action as to the remainder. The other sanctions—the investment bans, the transaction prohibitions, and the port-entry bans for RMRS-certified ships—all stay legally valid. RMRS remains a heavily sanctioned entity. It has simply defeated the mechanism the EU used to strip its regulatory status.
What the applicants argued
The applicants raised three main arguments. First, they said the measures were disproportionate. Shutting down RMRS’s operations, revoking its recognition, and blocking certified ships went, they argued, far beyond what the EU’s foreign-policy and security goals required.
The legal test is demanding for applicants. Restrictive measures must be appropriate and necessary to meet objectives of general interest. They must not impose a disproportionate burden. Yet RMRS is an instrument of the Russian state, and the Council generally enjoys a wide margin of appreciation in foreign and security policy.
(The court) orders the Council of the European Union and the Russian Maritime Register of Shipping to each bear their own costs. — Maria José Costeira, vice-president of the General Court of the European Union
Second, RMRS said the Council gave inadequate reasons under Article 296 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. It argued that a technical classification body deserved more than generic formulas about state ownership. EU institutions must state concrete grounds, so that the entity can defend its rights and the courts can review the decision.
Third, the applicants invoked the right to effective judicial review under Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. They said the design of the sanctions and the handling of evidence denied them a real chance to contest the designation. The court, for its part, must be able to verify the facts.
Who pays, and what comes next
On costs, nobody comes out ahead. Maria José Costeira, Vice-President of the General Court of the European Union, read out the order: “(The court) orders the Council of the European Union and the Russian Maritime Register of Shipping to each bear their own costs.” The European Commission, which supported the Council, must also bear its own costs.
Victories of this kind tend to be short-lived. When the General Court annuls a sanction, the Council rarely drops it. It usually corrects the flaws and reimposes the measure. It may redraft the statement of reasons with fresh evidence. It may also amend the framework to create broader categories, such as entities in high-revenue sectors like maritime transport.
The grace period exists to prevent a gap in sanctions coverage. The cycle of challenge and redrafting is a feature of the EU’s architecture. It lets the bloc wage economic warfare while showing that it respects judicial review and the rule of law.

The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “state of the climate” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets.
Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ask me anything” session.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.
This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.
The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.
Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.
Writing on CB Connect on 5 November, Hausfather wrote:
“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”
This year’s El Niño has already chalked up a number of milestones.
On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.
Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.
Membership
Support award-winning climate journalism
Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.
Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” analysis indicates that El Niño is set to continue to intensify into December, with 10 out of 14 models expecting temperatures in the Niño3.4 region to peak in the final month of this year. The remainder anticipate a November peak.
While human emissions of greenhouse gases are responsible for almost all of long-term global warming, temperatures in specific years are strongly influenced by El Niño events.
The “state of the climate” analysis explains that this year’s El Niño event will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. This is because global temperatures typically lag warming in the tropical Pacific by around three months.
Carbon Brief projects that the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels. It calculates a 96% chance that next year will be the warmest on record.
This projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions the preceding autumn. It also factors in uncertainty around how global temperatures will develop across the remainder of 2026.
